# Welcome to  
North East England

###### Our Region

## Welcome to our Awinspiring  
North East England region

To be fair, there are other English regions which also have captivating castles, luscious landscapes, amazing architecture and glorious gardens. And some English counties can also offer historic houses, wonderful walks, scintillating cities, festivals for foodies and museums to meander through.

But then there is **North East England.** Our region. Our beautiful, intriguing, complex, ever-fascinating corner of England which manages to offer all of the above and more. The complete package is here and what our region offers, it offers in real style.

Across the four English counties of Northumberland, County Durham, Tyne and Wear and Tees Valley you will find variety, quality, interest and opportunity. You will meet fun, friendly local people who have that unique personality and warm sense of humour which has become the trademark of our region.

![Image 5: Newcastle Gateshead](https://northeastenglandtouristguides.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Website-Landscape-62.png)

##### NewcastleGateshead &  
 North Tyneside

Do you want to pick up the pace and crank up the energy? A professionally guided NewcastleGateshead city tour will do just that whilst east of the city lies the coastal gems of North Tyneside.

[Learn More](https://northeastenglandtouristguides.co.uk/north-east-england/newcastlegateshead/)

![Image 7: Sunderland](https://northeastenglandtouristguides.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Website-Landscape-2021-01-18T130800.065.png)

##### Sunderland &  
 South Tyneside

The city of Sunderland and South Tyneside boast stunning architectural gems, fabulous beaches, amazing heritage and a whole lot more to discover with your Blue Badge Guide.

[Learn More](https://northeastenglandtouristguides.co.uk/north-east-england/sunderland/)

![Image 9: North East England: Durham](https://northeastenglandtouristguides.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/Images-landscape-for-web-2020-11-04T131539.899.png)

##### Durham City & the County Durham region

Explore stunning Durham City, its magnificent cathedral and castle before heading out on a discovery tour through County Durham’s rich heritage and landscape… You'll be amazed.

[Learn More](https://northeastenglandtouristguides.co.uk/north-east-england/durham/)

![Image 11: North East England: Northumberland & Hadrian's Wall](https://northeastenglandtouristguides.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/Images-landscape-for-web-27.png)

##### Northumberland

It’s official: Northumberland has been designated as the most tranquil county in England and the national park the best! Why? Find out with one of our professional tourist guides!

[Learn More](https://northeastenglandtouristguides.co.uk/north-east-england/northumberland/)

![Image 13: North East England: Tees Valley](https://northeastenglandtouristguides.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/Website-Landscape-14.png)

##### Teesside

Maritime heritage, modern art, stunning landscapes... Tees Valley has it all and North East England Tourist Guides will help you make most of your time here.

[Learn More](https://northeastenglandtouristguides.co.uk/north-east-england/teesside/)

![Image 15: North East England: Durham](https://northeastenglandtouristguides.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/Images-landscape-for-web-2020-11-04T131539.899.png)

##### Durham city & the County Durham region

Explore the stunning city of Durham and the surrounding county. Discover what makes Durham such a fabulous place with one of our dedicated Blue Badge tourist guides.

Learn More

###### Our Guides

## Explore North East England  
with a Blue Badge Tourist Guide

Our amazing North East England Blue Badge Guides can’t wait to meet you.

We can’t wait to see you stand on the very edge of the Roman Empire at Hadrian’s Wall World Heritage Site and hear you say how impressed you are by what you see. We want you to watch the fleeting performance of the mechanical Silver Swan at The Bowes Museum and see your reaction to the elegance of this remarkable automaton. We will show you where you can buy old fashioned confectionary at Beamish Museum the taste of which will take you right back to your childhood days. And we will take you to special, atmospheric locations such as the Holy Island of Lindisfarne, Jarrow and Durham where many centuries ago our Northern Saints once lived whilst doing their bit to shape early Christianity.

In our regional art galleries and museums we will stand beside you to explain the how, the why and the downright odd. **North East England**, often referred to as simply **the North East** within England, is one of nine official [regions of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regions_of_England "Regions of England"). It consists of [County Durham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Durham "County Durham"), [Northumberland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumberland "Northumberland"), [Tyne and Wear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyne_and_Wear "Tyne and Wear") and part of [North Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Yorkshire "North Yorkshire"). With 2.6 million residents in 2022, it is the least populous region of England. Its largest settlements include [Newcastle upon Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Newcastle upon Tyne"), [Sunderland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunderland "Sunderland"), [Middlesbrough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middlesbrough "Middlesbrough"), [Gateshead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gateshead "Gateshead"), [Darlington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darlington "Darlington") and [Hartlepool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartlepool "Hartlepool"). The North East is covered by two mayoral combined authorities: [North East Combined Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_Combined_Authority "North East Combined Authority") and [Tees Valley Combined Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tees_Valley_Combined_Authority "Tees Valley Combined Authority"). It is one of three regions, the other two being [North West England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_West_England "North West England") and [Yorkshire and the Humber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_and_the_Humber "Yorkshire and the Humber"), that make up [Northern England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_England "Northern England").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_East_England&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The region's historic importance is displayed by Northumberland's ancient castles, the two [World Heritage Sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Sites "World Heritage Sites") of [Durham Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham_Cathedral "Durham Cathedral") and [Durham Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham_Castle "Durham Castle"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-4) and [Hadrian's Wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadrian's_Wall "Hadrian's Wall"),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-5) one of the frontiers of the [Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire"). In fact, [Roman archaeology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_archaeology "Classical archaeology") can be found widely across the region and a special exhibition based around the Roman Fort of Segedunum at Wallsend[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-6) and the other forts along Hadrian's Wall are complemented by the numerous artefacts that are displayed in the Great North Museum Hancock[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-7) in Newcastle. [St. Peter's Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Peter's_Church,_Monkwearmouth "St Peter's Church, Monkwearmouth") in [Monkwearmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monkwearmouth "Monkwearmouth"), Sunderland and St. Pauls in [Jarrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jarrow "Jarrow") also hold significant historical value and have a joint bid to become a World Heritage Site.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-8)

The area has a strong religious past, as can be seen in works such as the _[Lindisfarne Gospels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindisfarne\_Gospels "Lindisfarne Gospels")_ and the _[Anglo-Saxon Chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxon\_Chronicle "Anglo-Saxon Chronicle")_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-9) The works of [Cuthbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert "Cuthbert") (634–687 AD), [Bede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bede "Bede") (673–735 AD) and [Hilda of Whitby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilda_of_Whitby "Hilda of Whitby") (614–680 AD) were hugely influential in the early church, and are still venerated by some today.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-11) These saints are usually associated with the monasteries on the island of [Lindisfarne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindisfarne "Lindisfarne"), [Wearmouth-Jarrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wearmouth-Jarrow "Wearmouth-Jarrow"), and the Abbey at [Whitby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitby "Whitby"), though they are also associated with many other religious sites in the region. Bede is regarded as the greatest Anglo-Saxon scholar. He worked at the monasteries of Wearmouth and Jarrow, translating some forty books on all areas of knowledge, including nature, history, astronomy, poetry and theological matters such as the lives of the saints. His best known work is "[The Ecclesiastical History of the English People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ecclesiastical_History_of_the_English_People "The Ecclesiastical History of the English People")".[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-12) One of the most famous pieces of art and literature created in the region is the _Lindisfarne Gospels_, thought to be the work of a monk named Eadfrith, who became Bishop of Lindisfarne in 698. This body of work is thought to have been created in honour of Cuthbert, around 710–720.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-13)

In 793, the Vikings arrived on the shores of north-east England with a raiding party from Norway who attacked the monastic settlement on Lindisfarne.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-14) The monks fled or were slaughtered, and Bishop Higbald sought refuge on the mainland. A chronicler recorded: "On the 8th June, the harrying of the heathen miserably destroyed God's church by rapine and slaughter." There were three hundred years of Viking raids, battles and settlement until [William the Conqueror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_the_Conqueror "William the Conqueror") defeated King Harold at Hastings in 1066.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-15) The _Anglo-Saxon Chronicle_ notes the change from raiding to settlement when it records that in 876 the Vikings "Shared out the land of the Northumbrians and they proceeded to plough and support themselves"[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-16)

The Anglo-Saxon Kingdom of Northumbria extended from the Scottish borders (then [Pictish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pictish "Pictish") borders) at the Firth of Forth to the north, and to the south of [York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York "York"), its capital, down to the Humber. The last independent Northumbrian king from 947–8 was [Eric Bloodaxe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Bloodaxe "Eric Bloodaxe"), who died at the [Battle of Stainmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Stainmore "Battle of Stainmore"), Westmorland, in 954. After Eric Bloodaxe's death, all England was ruled by [Eadred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eadred "Eadred"), the grandson of [Alfred the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_the_Great "Alfred the Great"); and so began the machinery of national government.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-17) Today, the Viking legacy can still be found in the language and place names of north-east England and in the [DNA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA "DNA") of its people.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-18) The name [Newcastle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Newcastle upon Tyne") comes from the castle built shortly after the conquest in 1080 by [Robert Curthose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Curthose "Robert Curthose"), William the Conqueror's eldest son.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-19)

Created in 1994, the region was defined as [Northumberland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumberland "Northumberland"), [Tyne and Wear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyne_and_Wear "Tyne and Wear"), [County Durham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Durham "County Durham") and [Cleveland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_(county) "Cleveland (county)"). A 1996 local-government reform created ceremonial counties and unitary authorities, allowing districts to govern outside their designated counties. The reform also abolished Cleveland with it split between County Durham and [North Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Yorkshire "North Yorkshire"), the latter county covers parts of two regions since.

The region is mostly parished with some remaining unparished areas following the 1974 creation of the Cleveland districts, [Darlington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borough_of_Darlington "Borough of Darlington"), Tyne and Wear districts, [Derwentside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derwentside "Derwentside") and [Wear Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wear_Valley "Wear Valley").

### Elections

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_East_England&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Elections")]

The North East has a strong tendency to vote [Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)"). In the [2015 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_United_Kingdom_general_election "2015 United Kingdom general election"), 47% of the electorate voted Labour, while 25% voted [Conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_(UK) "Conservative Party (UK)"), 17% UKIP, 6% [Liberal Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Democrats_(UK) "Liberal Democrats (UK)") and 4% Green. At the [2009 European election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_European_Parliament_election_in_the_United_Kingdom "2009 European Parliament election in the United Kingdom"), Labour got 25% of the region's vote, the Conservatives 20%, the Liberal Democrats 18%, and [UK Independence Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Independence_Party "UK Independence Party") 15%.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-20) However, in recent years, the North East has seen a significant swing away from Labour. In the 2019 election, many constituencies were targeted by the Conservatives and their representation increased to 10 MPs. The region wide vote shares were 43% for Labour and 38% for the Conservatives, with the [Brexit Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brexit_Party "Brexit Party") a distant third on 8%.

In November 2004, a [referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_North_East_England_devolution_referendum "2004 North East England devolution referendum") on whether a directly elected regional assembly should be set up for North East England resulted in a decisive "no" vote. The number of people who voted against the plans was 696,519 (78%), while 197,310 (22%) voted in favour. [John Prescott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Prescott "John Prescott"), the Deputy Prime Minister at the time, admitted that his plans for regional devolution had suffered an "emphatic defeat" to the no campaign, spearheaded by [Dominic Cummings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominic_Cummings "Dominic Cummings"). Bernard Jenkin, the Conservative spokesman for the regions, said the vote would mean the end of plans for a North East Assembly. He told the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC"): "The whole idea of regional government has been blown out of the water by this vote".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-21)

The former [Association of North East Councils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_North_East_Councils "Association of North East Councils") was based in [Newcastle upon Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Newcastle upon Tyne"), and the preceding [North East Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_Assembly "North East Assembly") was based in [Gateshead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gateshead "Gateshead") until its dissolution in 2009. [Local enterprise partnerships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_enterprise_partnership "Local enterprise partnership") were established, these later became combined authorities. The [North East Combined Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_Combined_Authority "North East Combined Authority") was established in 2014 and covered much of the region excluding [Tees Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tees_Valley "Tees Valley"). [North of Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_of_Tyne "North of Tyne") authorities later split off, leaving authorities south of the River Tyne.

The Tees Valley boroughs (Darlington, Hartlepool, Stockton-on-Tees, Redcar & Cleveland, and Middlesbrough) established the [Tees Valley Combined Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tees_Valley_Combined_Authority "Tees Valley Combined Authority") in 2016.

The region is generally hilly and sparsely populated in the North and West, and urban and arable in the East and South. The highest point in the region is [The Cheviot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cheviot "The Cheviot"), in the [Cheviot Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheviot_Hills "Cheviot Hills"), at 815 metres (2,674 ft).

The region contains the urban centres of [Tyneside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyneside "Tyneside"), [Wearside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wearside "Wearside"), and [Teesside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teesside "Teesside") and is noted for the rich natural beauty of its coastline, [Northumberland National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumberland_National_Park "Northumberland National Park"), and the section of the [Pennines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennines "Pennines") that includes [Teesdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teesdale "Teesdale") and [Weardale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weardale "Weardale").

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_East_England&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Climate")]

North East England has a [Marine west coast climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_climate "Oceanic climate") (generally found along the west coast of middle latitude continents) with narrower temperature ranges than the south of England and sufficient precipitation in all months. Summers and winters are mild rather than extremely hot or cold, due to the strong maritime influence of the [North Atlantic Current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Current "North Atlantic Current") of the [Gulf Stream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Stream "Gulf Stream"). The [Met Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Met_Office "Met Office") operates several weather stations in the region[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-22) and are able to show the regional variations in temperature and its relation to the distance from the [North Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Sea "North Sea"). The warmest summers in the region are found in Stockton-on-Tees and the [Middlesbrough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middlesbrough "Middlesbrough") area, with a 1981–2010 July average high of 20.4°C (68.7°F).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-23)

Precipitation is often low by English standards, in spite of the low levels of sunshine, with Stockton-on-Tees averaging only 574.2 millimetres (22.61 in) annually, and with the seaside town of Tynemouth (despite its slightly sunnier climate) recording 597.2 millimetres (23.51 in) annually.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-24) The summers on the northern coastlines are significantly cooler than in the southern and central inland areas: Tynemouth is only just above 18°C (64°F) in July. Further inland, frosts during winter are more common, due to the higher elevations and distance from the sea.

### Biodiversity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_East_England&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Biodiversity")]

The region has a diverse landscape that includes maritime cliffs and extensive [moorland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorland "Moorland") that contains a number of [rare species](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rare_species "Rare species") of [flora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flora "Flora") and [fauna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fauna "Fauna"). Of particular importance are the saltmarshes of [Lindisfarne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindisfarne "Lindisfarne"), the [Tees Estuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Tees "River Tees"), the [heaths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heaths "Heaths"), [bogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bog "Bog") and traditional upland hay meadows of the North Pennines, and the Arctic-alpine flora of Upper Teesdale.

The beauty of the [Northumbrian coastline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumberland_Coast_National_Landscape "Northumberland Coast National Landscape") has led to its designation as an [area of outstanding natural beauty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area_of_outstanding_natural_beauty "Area of outstanding natural beauty") (AONB) stretching 100 miles from [Berwick-Upon-Tweed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berwick-Upon-Tweed "Berwick-Upon-Tweed") to the [River Coquet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Coquet "River Coquet") estuary.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-25) Among the 290 bird species identified on the [Farne Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farne_Islands "Farne Islands"), is the rare [seabird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seabird "Seabird") the [roseate tern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roseate_tern "Roseate tern"). One of the foremost bird sanctuaries and observatory for migratory and wading birds in the UK is now operated at [Saltholme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saltholme "Saltholme") which is part of a wider site of special scientific interest called [Seal Sands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seal_Sands "Seal Sands"). The Saltholme reserve is managed by the [Royal Society for the Protection of Birds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Society_for_the_Protection_of_Birds "Royal Society for the Protection of Birds") (RSPB). This project was pronounced as one of the best places to view birds by [Bill Oddie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Oddie "Bill Oddie"), the former host of the BBC's _Spring Watch_ Programme. In December 2012 he also presented the project with a prize as the UK's favourite [National Lottery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Lottery_(United_Kingdom) "National Lottery (United Kingdom)") funded project.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-26)

The seal colony at Seal Sands on the mouth of the River Tees is thriving and in 2013 had more than 60 [harbour seals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harbour_seal "Harbour seal"). This is the only breeding colony of this species on the northeast coast.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-27) "[Rainton Meadows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainton_Meadows "Rainton Meadows")" is also a recently[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] created bird-watching site.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-28) The region is also the English stronghold of black grouse[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-29) and contains 80–90% of the UK population of yellow marsh [saxifrage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxifrage "Saxifrage").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-30)

The [Magnesian Limestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnesian_Limestone "Magnesian Limestone") grasslands of East Durham are a unique habitat not found anywhere else in the world which is particularly important to many species of butterfly and moths.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-31)

The Northeast of England also features woodland such as [Kielder Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kielder_Forest "Kielder Forest"), the largest man-made forest in Europe.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-32) This is located within Northumberland National Park and contains an important habitat for the [endangered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endangered "Endangered")[red squirrel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_squirrel "Red squirrel").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-33)

### Population genetics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_East_England&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Population genetics")]

North East England, together with Tweeddale, was the ancient British tribal kingdom of [Bernicia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernicia "Bernicia") (Bryneich) and is notable for providing the stable ancestry of its present indigenous population, which has been identified by DNA analysis to be an offshoot of the group "Scotland, Cumbria and the North of Ireland", but not so closely related to the other peoples of the UK.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-47) In a 2022 study by Joscha Gretzinger et al., the population of North East England was found to be among the groups with the highest amount of Iron Age/Roman period [British Isles-related](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insular_Celts "Insular Celts") ancestry, being on par with [Cornish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornish_people "Cornish people") people in that regard.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-48)

### Social deprivation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_East_England&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Social deprivation")]

A study into social deprivation was published in 2010 to help the local partners developing a Regional Strategy for the North East better understand the factors influencing deprivation in the region. The study had two main aspects: Firstly to establish if there are different types of deprived neighbourhoods in the Northeast, and if so, how deprived neighbourhoods can be better recognised. Secondly to present a summary of "what works" in tackling deprivation in each of these types of area.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-51)

The report discusses the factors influencing deprivation and points out that it is a significant problem for the North East with 34% of the regions Lower Super Output Areas (LSOAs) are amongst England's 20% most deprived in the 2007 [Indices of Deprivation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indices_of_deprivation_2007 "Indices of deprivation 2007") (these indices have been [updated in 2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indices_of_deprivation_2010 "Indices of deprivation 2010")). It takes many years for areas to become deprived, suggesting that the underlying causes of area-based deprivation are long-term such as:

*   Major changes in the employment base, which has changed the nature and spatial distribution of jobs in the UK and within specific regions and localities.
*   The "residential sorting" effects of the public and private housing markets.

Industrial restructuring has disproportionately affected some communities and groups. In particular:

*   Job losses in manufacturing and coalmining were most severely felt in the north of England, Scotland and Wales – and particular communities within these areas.
*   As a result of the types of jobs that were lost, some demographic groups – particularly older working age males in skilled manual work – were more likely to be affected than others.[_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_]

The region's most deprived council districts, as measured by the LSOA data[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-52) before County Durham and Northumberland became unitary authorities in 2007, are in descending order [Easington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easington_(district) "Easington (district)") (7th in England), Middlesbrough (9th), Hartlepool (23rd), [Wear Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wear_Valley "Wear Valley") (33rd), Sunderland (35th), Newcastle upon Tyne (37th), South Tyneside (38th), Wansbeck (46th), Redcar and Cleveland (50th), Gateshead (52nd), [Sedgefield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sedgefield_(borough) "Sedgefield (borough)") (54th), [Derwentside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derwentside "Derwentside") (73rd), [Blyth Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blyth_Valley "Blyth Valley") (80th), and Stockton on Tees (98th). The least deprived council districts in 2007 were, in descending order, Tynedale, [Castle Morpeth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_Morpeth "Castle Morpeth"), [Teesdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teesdale_(district) "Teesdale (district)"), then [Alnwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alnwick_(district) "Alnwick (district)"). Since the April 2009 abolition of these four districts, Northumberland is the least deprived, followed by North Tyneside. Unemployment is a severe problem in the North East, where many children grow up in households where no adult works. In 2010 Easington had the highest rate in the country, as 40.3% of its households with children had no working adult, followed by Sedgefield with 34%.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_][_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_]

As of April 2013, youth unemployment in the North East was 24.8%, with 51,000 out of work.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-53) In 2013, the Office for National Statistics report issued the statements highlighted in the table below:[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-54)

**North East England**, often referred to as simply **the North East** within England, is one of nine official [regions of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regions_of_England "Regions of England"). It consists of [County Durham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Durham "County Durham"), [Northumberland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumberland "Northumberland"), [Tyne and Wear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyne_and_Wear "Tyne and Wear") and part of [North Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Yorkshire "North Yorkshire"). With 2.6 million residents in 2022, it is the least populous region of England. Its largest settlements include [Newcastle upon Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Newcastle upon Tyne"), [Sunderland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunderland "Sunderland"), [Middlesbrough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middlesbrough "Middlesbrough"), [Gateshead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gateshead "Gateshead"), [Darlington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darlington "Darlington") and [Hartlepool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartlepool "Hartlepool"). The North East is covered by two mayoral combined authorities: [North East Combined Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_Combined_Authority "North East Combined Authority") and [Tees Valley Combined Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tees_Valley_Combined_Authority "Tees Valley Combined Authority"). It is one of three regions, the other two being [North West England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_West_England "North West England") and [Yorkshire and the Humber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_and_the_Humber "Yorkshire and the Humber"), that make up [Northern England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_England "Northern England").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_East_England&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The region's historic importance is displayed by Northumberland's ancient castles, the two [World Heritage Sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Sites "World Heritage Sites") of [Durham Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham_Cathedral "Durham Cathedral") and [Durham Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham_Castle "Durham Castle"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-4) and [Hadrian's Wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadrian's_Wall "Hadrian's Wall"),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-5) one of the frontiers of the [Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire"). In fact, [Roman archaeology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_archaeology "Classical archaeology") can be found widely across the region and a special exhibition based around the Roman Fort of Segedunum at Wallsend[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-6) and the other forts along Hadrian's Wall are complemented by the numerous artefacts that are displayed in the Great North Museum Hancock[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-7) in Newcastle. [St. Peter's Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Peter's_Church,_Monkwearmouth "St Peter's Church, Monkwearmouth") in [Monkwearmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monkwearmouth "Monkwearmouth"), Sunderland and St. Pauls in [Jarrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jarrow "Jarrow") also hold significant historical value and have a joint bid to become a World Heritage Site.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-8)

The area has a strong religious past, as can be seen in works such as the _[Lindisfarne Gospels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindisfarne\_Gospels "Lindisfarne Gospels")_ and the _[Anglo-Saxon Chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxon\_Chronicle "Anglo-Saxon Chronicle")_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-9) The works of [Cuthbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert "Cuthbert") (634–687 AD), [Bede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bede "Bede") (673–735 AD) and [Hilda of Whitby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilda_of_Whitby "Hilda of Whitby") (614–680 AD) were hugely influential in the early church, and are still venerated by some today.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-11) These saints are usually associated with the monasteries on the island of [Lindisfarne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindisfarne "Lindisfarne"), [Wearmouth-Jarrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wearmouth-Jarrow "Wearmouth-Jarrow"), and the Abbey at [Whitby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitby "Whitby"), though they are also associated with many other religious sites in the region. Bede is regarded as the greatest Anglo-Saxon scholar. He worked at the monasteries of Wearmouth and Jarrow, translating some forty books on all areas of knowledge, including nature, history, astronomy, poetry and theological matters such as the lives of the saints. His best known work is "[The Ecclesiastical History of the English People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ecclesiastical_History_of_the_English_People "The Ecclesiastical History of the English People")".[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-12) One of the most famous pieces of art and literature created in the region is the _Lindisfarne Gospels_, thought to be the work of a monk named Eadfrith, who became Bishop of Lindisfarne in 698. This body of work is thought to have been created in honour of Cuthbert, around 710–720.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-13)

In 793, the Vikings arrived on the shores of north-east England with a raiding party from Norway who attacked the monastic settlement on Lindisfarne.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-14) The monks fled or were slaughtered, and Bishop Higbald sought refuge on the mainland. A chronicler recorded: "On the 8th June, the harrying of the heathen miserably destroyed God's church by rapine and slaughter." There were three hundred years of Viking raids, battles and settlement until [William the Conqueror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_the_Conqueror "William the Conqueror") defeated King Harold at Hastings in 1066.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-15) The _Anglo-Saxon Chronicle_ notes the change from raiding to settlement when it records that in 876 the Vikings "Shared out the land of the Northumbrians and they proceeded to plough and support themselves"[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-16)

The Anglo-Saxon Kingdom of Northumbria extended from the Scottish borders (then [Pictish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pictish "Pictish") borders) at the Firth of Forth to the north, and to the south of [York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York "York"), its capital, down to the Humber. The last independent Northumbrian king from 947–8 was [Eric Bloodaxe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Bloodaxe "Eric Bloodaxe"), who died at the [Battle of Stainmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Stainmore "Battle of Stainmore"), Westmorland, in 954. After Eric Bloodaxe's death, all England was ruled by [Eadred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eadred "Eadred"), the grandson of [Alfred the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_the_Great "Alfred the Great"); and so began the machinery of national government.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-17) Today, the Viking legacy can still be found in the language and place names of north-east England and in the [DNA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA "DNA") of its people.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-18) The name [Newcastle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Newcastle upon Tyne") comes from the castle built shortly after the conquest in 1080 by [Robert Curthose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Curthose "Robert Curthose"), William the Conqueror's eldest son.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-19)

Created in 1994, the region was defined as [Northumberland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumberland "Northumberland"), [Tyne and Wear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyne_and_Wear "Tyne and Wear"), [County Durham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Durham "County Durham") and [Cleveland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_(county) "Cleveland (county)"). A 1996 local-government reform created ceremonial counties and unitary authorities, allowing districts to govern outside their designated counties. The reform also abolished Cleveland with it split between County Durham and [North Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Yorkshire "North Yorkshire"), the latter county covers parts of two regions since.

The region is mostly parished with some remaining unparished areas following the 1974 creation of the Cleveland districts, [Darlington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borough_of_Darlington "Borough of Darlington"), Tyne and Wear districts, [Derwentside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derwentside "Derwentside") and [Wear Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wear_Valley "Wear Valley").

### Elections

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_East_England&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Elections")]

The North East has a strong tendency to vote [Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)"). In the [2015 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_United_Kingdom_general_election "2015 United Kingdom general election"), 47% of the electorate voted Labour, while 25% voted [Conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_(UK) "Conservative Party (UK)"), 17% UKIP, 6% [Liberal Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Democrats_(UK) "Liberal Democrats (UK)") and 4% Green. At the [2009 European election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_European_Parliament_election_in_the_United_Kingdom "2009 European Parliament election in the United Kingdom"), Labour got 25% of the region's vote, the Conservatives 20%, the Liberal Democrats 18%, and [UK Independence Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Independence_Party "UK Independence Party") 15%.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-20) However, in recent years, the North East has seen a significant swing away from Labour. In the 2019 election, many constituencies were targeted by the Conservatives and their representation increased to 10 MPs. The region wide vote shares were 43% for Labour and 38% for the Conservatives, with the [Brexit Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brexit_Party "Brexit Party") a distant third on 8%.

In November 2004, a [referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_North_East_England_devolution_referendum "2004 North East England devolution referendum") on whether a directly elected regional assembly should be set up for North East England resulted in a decisive "no" vote. The number of people who voted against the plans was 696,519 (78%), while 197,310 (22%) voted in favour. [John Prescott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Prescott "John Prescott"), the Deputy Prime Minister at the time, admitted that his plans for regional devolution had suffered an "emphatic defeat" to the no campaign, spearheaded by [Dominic Cummings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominic_Cummings "Dominic Cummings"). Bernard Jenkin, the Conservative spokesman for the regions, said the vote would mean the end of plans for a North East Assembly. He told the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC"): "The whole idea of regional government has been blown out of the water by this vote".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-21)

The former [Association of North East Councils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_North_East_Councils "Association of North East Councils") was based in [Newcastle upon Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Newcastle upon Tyne"), and the preceding [North East Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_Assembly "North East Assembly") was based in [Gateshead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gateshead "Gateshead") until its dissolution in 2009. [Local enterprise partnerships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_enterprise_partnership "Local enterprise partnership") were established, these later became combined authorities. The [North East Combined Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_Combined_Authority "North East Combined Authority") was established in 2014 and covered much of the region excluding [Tees Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tees_Valley "Tees Valley"). [North of Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_of_Tyne "North of Tyne") authorities later split off, leaving authorities south of the River Tyne.

The Tees Valley boroughs (Darlington, Hartlepool, Stockton-on-Tees, Redcar & Cleveland, and Middlesbrough) established the [Tees Valley Combined Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tees_Valley_Combined_Authority "Tees Valley Combined Authority") in 2016.

The region is generally hilly and sparsely populated in the North and West, and urban and arable in the East and South. The highest point in the region is [The Cheviot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cheviot "The Cheviot"), in the [Cheviot Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheviot_Hills "Cheviot Hills"), at 815 metres (2,674 ft).

The region contains the urban centres of [Tyneside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyneside "Tyneside"), [Wearside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wearside "Wearside"), and [Teesside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teesside "Teesside") and is noted for the rich natural beauty of its coastline, [Northumberland National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumberland_National_Park "Northumberland National Park"), and the section of the [Pennines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennines "Pennines") that includes [Teesdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teesdale "Teesdale") and [Weardale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weardale "Weardale").

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_East_England&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Climate")]

North East England has a [Marine west coast climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_climate "Oceanic climate") (generally found along the west coast of middle latitude continents) with narrower temperature ranges than the south of England and sufficient precipitation in all months. Summers and winters are mild rather than extremely hot or cold, due to the strong maritime influence of the [North Atlantic Current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Current "North Atlantic Current") of the [Gulf Stream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Stream "Gulf Stream"). The [Met Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Met_Office "Met Office") operates several weather stations in the region[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-22) and are able to show the regional variations in temperature and its relation to the distance from the [North Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Sea "North Sea"). The warmest summers in the region are found in Stockton-on-Tees and the [Middlesbrough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middlesbrough "Middlesbrough") area, with a 1981–2010 July average high of 20.4°C (68.7°F).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-23)

Precipitation is often low by English standards, in spite of the low levels of sunshine, with Stockton-on-Tees averaging only 574.2 millimetres (22.61 in) annually, and with the seaside town of Tynemouth (despite its slightly sunnier climate) recording 597.2 millimetres (23.51 in) annually.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-24) The summers on the northern coastlines are significantly cooler than in the southern and central inland areas: Tynemouth is only just above 18°C (64°F) in July. Further inland, frosts during winter are more common, due to the higher elevations and distance from the sea.

### Biodiversity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_East_England&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Biodiversity")]

The region has a diverse landscape that includes maritime cliffs and extensive [moorland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorland "Moorland") that contains a number of [rare species](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rare_species "Rare species") of [flora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flora "Flora") and [fauna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fauna "Fauna"). Of particular importance are the saltmarshes of [Lindisfarne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindisfarne "Lindisfarne"), the [Tees Estuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Tees "River Tees"), the [heaths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heaths "Heaths"), [bogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bog "Bog") and traditional upland hay meadows of the North Pennines, and the Arctic-alpine flora of Upper Teesdale.

The beauty of the [Northumbrian coastline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumberland_Coast_National_Landscape "Northumberland Coast National Landscape") has led to its designation as an [area of outstanding natural beauty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area_of_outstanding_natural_beauty "Area of outstanding natural beauty") (AONB) stretching 100 miles from [Berwick-Upon-Tweed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berwick-Upon-Tweed "Berwick-Upon-Tweed") to the [River Coquet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Coquet "River Coquet") estuary.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-25) Among the 290 bird species identified on the [Farne Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farne_Islands "Farne Islands"), is the rare [seabird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seabird "Seabird") the [roseate tern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roseate_tern "Roseate tern"). One of the foremost bird sanctuaries and observatory for migratory and wading birds in the UK is now operated at [Saltholme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saltholme "Saltholme") which is part of a wider site of special scientific interest called [Seal Sands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seal_Sands "Seal Sands"). The Saltholme reserve is managed by the [Royal Society for the Protection of Birds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Society_for_the_Protection_of_Birds "Royal Society for the Protection of Birds") (RSPB). This project was pronounced as one of the best places to view birds by [Bill Oddie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Oddie "Bill Oddie"), the former host of the BBC's _Spring Watch_ Programme. In December 2012 he also presented the project with a prize as the UK's favourite [National Lottery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Lottery_(United_Kingdom) "National Lottery (United Kingdom)") funded project.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-26)

The seal colony at Seal Sands on the mouth of the River Tees is thriving and in 2013 had more than 60 [harbour seals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harbour_seal "Harbour seal"). This is the only breeding colony of this species on the northeast coast.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-27) "[Rainton Meadows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainton_Meadows "Rainton Meadows")" is also a recently[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] created bird-watching site.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-28) The region is also the English stronghold of black grouse[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-29) and contains 80–90% of the UK population of yellow marsh [saxifrage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxifrage "Saxifrage").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-30)

The [Magnesian Limestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnesian_Limestone "Magnesian Limestone") grasslands of East Durham are a unique habitat not found anywhere else in the world which is particularly important to many species of butterfly and moths.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-31)

The Northeast of England also features woodland such as [Kielder Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kielder_Forest "Kielder Forest"), the largest man-made forest in Europe.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-32) This is located within Northumberland National Park and contains an important habitat for the [endangered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endangered "Endangered")[red squirrel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_squirrel "Red squirrel").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-33)

The North East has the smallest population of all English regions.

The North East with [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland"), the [South West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_West_England "South West England") of England, [Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales "Wales") and [Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland "Northern Ireland") are the British regions to have seen the least immigration in over 50 years.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-34)[_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] The Northeast of England as a region has the lowest rate of HIV infection in the UK,[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-35) but has the highest rate of heart attacks among men and of lung cancer among women in England, along with the highest male lung cancer rate in the UK.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-36)

Higher education students from the North East are most likely to pick a university in their home region.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-38) The last immigration wave before the 21st century was in the late 1990s as a result of the government's dispersal policy scheme that relocated asylum seekers and new arrivals throughout the country. In 2017, most migrants were non-EU born, and about 60,000 EU-born.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-39)

### Population genetics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_East_England&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Population genetics")]

North East England, together with Tweeddale, was the ancient British tribal kingdom of [Bernicia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernicia "Bernicia") (Bryneich) and is notable for providing the stable ancestry of its present indigenous population, which has been identified by DNA analysis to be an offshoot of the group "Scotland, Cumbria and the North of Ireland", but not so closely related to the other peoples of the UK.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-47) In a 2022 study by Joscha Gretzinger et al., the population of North East England was found to be among the groups with the highest amount of Iron Age/Roman period [British Isles-related](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insular_Celts "Insular Celts") ancestry, being on par with [Cornish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornish_people "Cornish people") people in that regard.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-48)

The Office for National Statistics in April 2013 report that the estimated number of conceptions to women aged under 18 in England and Wales in 2011 is the lowest since records began in 1969.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-Office_for_National_Statistics-49) Conception statistics include pregnancies that result in either one or more live births or stillbirths or a legal abortion.

A comparison of rates across regions in England shows that the North East had the highest of under 18 conception rates in 2021, with 19.8 conceptions per thousand women aged under 18 years, despite nearly halving since 2011. London had the lowest rate for women aged under 18 in 2021 with 9.5 conceptions per thousand women aged under 18.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-50)

### Social deprivation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_East_England&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Social deprivation")]

A study into social deprivation was published in 2010 to help the local partners developing a Regional Strategy for the North East better understand the factors influencing deprivation in the region. The study had two main aspects: Firstly to establish if there are different types of deprived neighbourhoods in the Northeast, and if so, how deprived neighbourhoods can be better recognised. Secondly to present a summary of "what works" in tackling deprivation in each of these types of area.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-51)

The report discusses the factors influencing deprivation and points out that it is a significant problem for the North East with 34% of the regions Lower Super Output Areas (LSOAs) are amongst England's 20% most deprived in the 2007 [Indices of Deprivation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indices_of_deprivation_2007 "Indices of deprivation 2007") (these indices have been [updated in 2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indices_of_deprivation_2010 "Indices of deprivation 2010")). It takes many years for areas to become deprived, suggesting that the underlying causes of area-based deprivation are long-term such as:

*   Major changes in the employment base, which has changed the nature and spatial distribution of jobs in the UK and within specific regions and localities.
*   The "residential sorting" effects of the public and private housing markets.

Industrial restructuring has disproportionately affected some communities and groups. In particular:

*   Job losses in manufacturing and coalmining were most severely felt in the north of England, Scotland and Wales – and particular communities within these areas.
*   As a result of the types of jobs that were lost, some demographic groups – particularly older working age males in skilled manual work – were more likely to be affected than others.[_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_]

The region's most deprived council districts, as measured by the LSOA data[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-52) before County Durham and Northumberland became unitary authorities in 2007, are in descending order [Easington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easington_(district) "Easington (district)") (7th in England), Middlesbrough (9th), Hartlepool (23rd), [Wear Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wear_Valley "Wear Valley") (33rd), Sunderland (35th), Newcastle upon Tyne (37th), South Tyneside (38th), Wansbeck (46th), Redcar and Cleveland (50th), Gateshead (52nd), [Sedgefield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sedgefield_(borough) "Sedgefield (borough)") (54th), [Derwentside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derwentside "Derwentside") (73rd), [Blyth Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blyth_Valley "Blyth Valley") (80th), and Stockton on Tees (98th). The least deprived council districts in 2007 were, in descending order, Tynedale, [Castle Morpeth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_Morpeth "Castle Morpeth"), [Teesdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teesdale_(district) "Teesdale (district)"), then [Alnwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alnwick_(district) "Alnwick (district)"). Since the April 2009 abolition of these four districts, Northumberland is the least deprived, followed by North Tyneside. Unemployment is a severe problem in the North East, where many children grow up in households where no adult works. In 2010 Easington had the highest rate in the country, as 40.3% of its households with children had no working adult, followed by Sedgefield with 34%.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_][_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_]

As of April 2013, youth unemployment in the North East was 24.8%, with 51,000 out of work.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-53) In 2013, the Office for National Statistics report issued the statements highlighted in the table below:[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-54)

The North East compared to other regions in 2013| Rate | Highest | Lowest |

| Inactive | _North East (25.8%)_ | South East (19.8%) |
| Claimant | _North East (7.2%)_ | South East (2.7%) |

In November 2017 the region's employment dropped to 5.5%, the joint highest unemployment rate in the UK.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England#cite_note-55)

1.  INTRODUCTION

1.1.  BACKGROUND
1.1.1.  This Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Scoping Report constitutes a request to
Rushmoor Borough Council (RBC) for its formal opinion on the scope, level of detail
and methodology of the information to be provided in the Environmental Statement
(ES), which will accompany a planning application to be made by Farnborough Airport
Limited (hereafter referred to as ‘the Applicant’).
1.1.2.  The Applicant is seeking permission to change the existing planning conditions under
which Farnborough Airport (hereafter referred to as ‘the Airport’) operates.
1.1.3.  In Autumn 2023, the Applicant consulted on its long-term future and subsequently
submitted a planning application to increase its allowable flights from 50,000 to
70,000 per annum (Planning Reference: 23/00794/REVPP). This is known and ‘the
2023 Planning Application’.
1.1.4.  Since submitting the 2023 Planning Application, the Applicant has been working with
stakeholders on several technical matters which has involved responding to
consultation with statutory consultees. Naturally these processes can be extremely
lengthy, and as a result more time will be required to bring these discussions to a
satisfactory conclusion.
1.1.5.  For this reason, the Applicant has decided to consult on a new Proposal which will
support the Airport’s medium-term growth requirements without jeopardising its long-
term future.
1.1.6.  As part of this Proposal, the Applicant is seeking to increase non-weekday (i.e.
weekends and public holidays) aircraft movements at the Airport within its current limit
of 50,000 aircraft movements per annum (pa), amend the maximum take-off weight
(MTOW) categories, and amend the conditions related to airport public safety zones
(PSZs) in line with the latest Government guidance, by varying the conditions
attached to planning permission reference 20/00871/REVPP1 (hereafter referred to as
‘the Proposal’). Amending these conditions would enable the Airport to continue to
meet future market demand for business aviation activity.
1.1.7.  The 'Site' referred to in this Report is the land within the Airport boundary of
ownership as defined in Figure 2.1: Site Location Plan of Appendix A, with the red
line illustrating the extent of the Site which is hereafter referred to as the 'Site
Boundary'.

1.3.  DEFINITION OF AN EIA
1.3.1.  The term EIA describes a procedure that must be followed for certain types of
projects before they can be given consent. The procedure is a means of drawing
together, in a systematic way, an assessment of a project’s potential significant
environmental effects. This helps to ensure that the importance of the predicted
effects and the scope for avoiding, preventing, reducing or, if possible, offsetting them
are properly understood by the public and the authority granting consent (the
'determining authority') before it makes its decision.

amended/codified by Directives 97/11/EC6, 2003/35/EC7, 2011/92/EU8 and
2014/52/EU9) which is transposed into UK legislation. The regulations specific to
applications made under the TCPA 19902 are the EIA Regulations3.

1.4.2.  The first stage of the EIA process is to screen whether a proposed development
triggers the need for an EIA against the descriptions given in Schedule 1 and 2 of the
EIA Regulations3. For developments listed under Schedule 1 of the EIA Regulations,
an EIA is mandatory. If a project is listed in Schedule 2, an EIA is required where it is
considered to have likely significant effects on the environment by virtue of factors
such as its nature, size or location drawing on Schedule 3.
1.4.3.  The Proposal has the potential to have significant effects on the environment, due to
its characteristics and location, and is an application under Section 73 of the TCPA
19902 relating to EIA development. Therefore, the Proposal falls under Schedule 2
(Paragraph 13a(i)) of the EIA Regulations3.

1.4.4.  The Applicant is preparing an ES to ensure that the likely significant effects on the
environment resulting from the Proposal are considered and, where appropriate,
mitigated.

scope and level of detail of the information to be provided in the ES.

2.  DESCRIPTION OF THE PROPOSAL

2.1.  DESCRIPTION OF THE SITE AND EXISTING OPERATIONS
2.1.1.  The Airport is located adjacent to and west of the settlement of Farnborough, within
the Borough of Rushmoor in Hampshire (see Figure 2.1: Site Location Plan of
Appendix A: Figures). The Airport provides business aviation services and
predominantly operates small to medium sized aircraft. The Airport is bounded by the
A327 and Elles Road providing access to the north, the A325 to the east, Aerospace
Boulevard to the south and the A323 (Fleet Road), Ively Road and Old Ively Road to
the west. These roads serve a number of commercial and retail properties such as
Cody Technology Park to the North, Farnborough Business Park to the east, and one
to the south that comprises of 10 business premises. The residential wards within
RBC around the Airport include St Mark’s, Cove and Southwood, Empress,
Knellwood and Wellington, which have a combined population of approximately
38,62010.

2.1.2.  The Airport is approximately 239 hectares in size and comprises predominantly of
managed modified grassland and concreted areas such as runway, taxiways, and
aircraft stands. There is also a car park, a large modern terminal building, several
large aircraft hangars, an air traffic control tower, a fire station, a fuel depot,
commercial buildings and a 169-bedroom hotel with leisure and conference facilities.

2.1.18.  There is one runway at the Airport with two directions of use. The direction of arrivals

east and ‘westerly operations’ when the wind direction is from the west. The UK’s
prevailing wind is from a south westerly direction, meaning the Airport operates on
westerly operations for most of the time. The split between westerly and easterly
operations varies year to year, however over the last three years (2022 to 2024)
westerly operations have occurred on average approximately 75% of the time
meaning the arrivals and departures to the east have occurred around 25% of the
time.

OVERARCHING AVIATION NOISE POLICY (2023)
3.5.4.  The Overarching Aviation Noise Policy Statement (OANPS)46 was published on 27
March 2023 and details the Government’s revised overarching aviation noise policy
statement. Its revision is linked to the  Flightpath to the Future47, which acknowledged
that the Government would set out next steps on noise policy in 2022 to 2023.
3.5.5.  The publication of the OANPS46 supported the night-time noise abatement objective
consultation whilst providing clarity for both airports and their stakeholders when
preparing or responding to noise action plan consultations.
3.5.6.  The OANPS46 sets out the Government’s revised overarching aviation noise policy
relating to aviation, as follows:
“The Government’s overall policy on aviation noise is to balance the economic and
consumer benefits of aviation against their social and health implications in line with
the International Civil Aviation Organisation’s Balanced Approach to Aircraft Noise
Management. This should take into account the local and national context of both
passenger and freight operations and recognise the additional health impacts of night
flights. The impact of aviation noise must be mitigated as much as is practicable and
realistic to do so, limiting, and where possible reducing, the total adverse impacts on
health and quality of life from aviation noise”.
3.5.7.  The OANPS46 also refers to a previous consultation, as part of  Aviation 205048, on
setting a new objective “to limit, and where possible, reduce total adverse effects on
health and quality of life from aviation noise”48. The OANPS explains:

“We consider that “limit, and where possible reduce” remains appropriate wording. An
overall reduction in total adverse effects is desirable, but in the context of sustainable
growth an increase in total adverse effects may be offset by an increase in econ  omic

CURRENT STATE OF THE ENVIRONMENT
4.3.1.  Baseline environmental conditions need to be established to enable an accurate
assessment of potential changes to such conditions which may occur and to assess
the potential significant environmental effects of the Proposal. Understanding baseline
conditions is also important for the identification of the most appropriate
environmental measures which could be adopted to reduce any potential significant
adverse effects.
4.3.2.  The EIA Regulations3 require an ES to describe the current state of the environment.
This information will be gathered through desk-based research, site surveys and
information available at the time of the assessment, to define and describe the
existing environmental characteristics and receptors for each environmental
discipline.
4.3.3.  Operational data from 2024 will generally be used to describe the current state of the
environment to provide a typical description of the Airport’s operations. There may be
some situations, namely traffic and transport, where the current state of the
environment will be extrapolated using a growth forecast on existing survey data.

4.3.4.  It is recognised that the Airport is not operating at the approved 50,000 aircraft
movements pa. Therefore, should the EIA compare the environmental effects of the
proposed 13,500 aircraft movements pa during non-weekdays to the current state of
the environment, it would not be clear which part of the environmental effect resulted
from increasing the non-weekday cap on aircraft movements and which part related to
expanded operations within the existing cap.
4.3.5.  The EIA Regulations3 require an outline of the likely evolution of the baseline
conditions without implementation of the Proposal. Future baseline conditions and
appropriate assumptions will be used to inform the EIA in assessing likely future
conditions should the Proposal not proceed. This is termed as the ‘Without Proposal’
scenario. The future baseline conditions will be described in each technical chapter of
the ES.
4.3.6.  As such, and to provide a transparent assessment, the 'With Proposal’ and ‘Without
Proposal’ scenarios will be identified to underpin the EIA. These scenarios will be
based on the most robust data available and based on the Applicant’s projections for
growth, policy outlined in Section 3.3, market signals and professional judgement
through consultation with recognised industry experts.
4.3.7.  The scenarios will clearly set out how operations at the Airport will likely evolve based
firstly on the 2011 Planning Permission17 (the ‘Without Proposal’ scenario) and
secondly with the Proposal (the  ‘With Proposal’ scenario), see below for further
details. Comparing the With Proposal scenario with the Without Proposal scenario will
allow the effects of the Proposal to be readily identified for each assessment year.
4.3.8.  Data for the Without Proposal scenario will be used as the basis of the assessment
for relevant assessment years. Future baseline conditions will be identified through
modelling/predictions to identify future environmental conditions that can form the
basis to assess the future effects of the Proposal. For example, the noise assessment
will predict noise conditions at and in the vicinity of the Airport for the Without
Proposal scenario. These noise conditions will then be compared with the noise
conditions in the same year for the With Proposal scenario to identify the potential
significant effects of the Proposal for that year.

4.6.  APPROACH TO MITIGATION
4.6.1.  Regulation 18(3)(c) of the EIA Regulations3 requires an ES to include:

“A description of any features of the proposed development, or measures envisaged
in order to avoid, prevent or reduce and, if possible, offset potential significant
adverse effects on the environment”.
4.6.2.  Paragraph 7 of Schedule 4 to the EIA Regulations3 provides further specification of
the information on mitigation measures to be included in an ES:
“A description of the measures envisaged to avoid, prevent, reduce or, if possible,
offset any identified significant adverse effects on the environment and, where
appropriate, of any proposed monitoring arrangements (for example the preparation
of a post-project analysis). That description should explain the extent, to which
significant adverse effects on the environment are avoided, prevented, reduced or
offset, and should cover both the construction and operational phases”.
4.6.3.  The assessments reported in the ES will be used to identify the mitigation required to
avoid, prevent, reduce or, if possible, offset any identified significant adverse effects
on the environment. Such mitigation will be described accordingly in the ES.

significant adverse effects that arise as a result of a proposed development. Each
respective section of the ES will set out in detail monitoring arrangements where

4.8.  APPROACH TO THE ASSESSMENT OF CUMULATIVE EFFECTS
4.8.1.  The ES will include an assessment of potential cumulative effects taking into account
the relevant regulations and guidance as set out above and using the methodology
detailed in this section of the Scoping Report.
4.8.2.  Paragraph 5(e) of Schedule 4 of the EIA Regulations3 refers to the need to consider:

“The cumulation of effects with other existing and/or approved projects, taking into
account any existing environmental problems relating to areas of particular
environmental importance likely to be affected or the use of natural resources”.
4.8.3.  The requirement to consider ‘existing and/or approved’ development is echoed within
the EIA Planning Practice Guidance78, which notes in Paragraph 024:

“There are occasions, however, when other existing or approved development may
be relevant in determining whether significant effects are likely as a consequence of a
proposed development. The local planning authorities should always have regard to
the possible cumulative effects arising from any existing or approved development”.
4.8.4.  Two types of cumulative effects will be considered in the ES:
•  Inter-Project Cumulative Effects – The combined residual (post-mitigation)
environmental effects of the Proposal with a committed project (or projects)
affecting the same receptor; and
•  Intra-Project Combined Effects – The interaction and combination of different
residual (post-mitigation) environmental effects of the Proposal affecting the same
receptor.

INTER-PROJECT CUMULATIVE EFFECTS ASSESSMENT
4.8.5.  There is no standard methodology or widely agreed upon best practice for the
assessment of cumulative effects. The methodology that will be adopted for the
assessment of the Proposal is based on professional judgement and the approach
that was taken for the cumulative effects assessment for the 2011 Planning
Permission17.

1.  INTRODUCTION

1.1.  BACKGROUND
1.1.1.  This Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Scoping Report constitutes a request to
Rushmoor Borough Council (RBC) for its formal opinion on the scope, level of detail
and methodology of the information to be provided in the Environmental Statement
(ES), which will accompany a planning application to be made by Farnborough Airport
Limited (hereafter referred to as ‘the Applicant’).
1.1.2.  The Applicant is seeking permission to change the existing planning conditions under
which Farnborough Airport (hereafter referred to as ‘the Airport’) operates.
1.1.3.  In Autumn 2023, the Applicant consulted on its long-term future and subsequently
submitted a planning application to increase its allowable flights from 50,000 to
70,000 per annum (Planning Reference: 23/00794/REVPP). This is known and ‘the
2023 Planning Application’.
1.1.4.  Since submitting the 2023 Planning Application, the Applicant has been working with
stakeholders on several technical matters which has involved responding to
consultation with statutory consultees. Naturally these processes can be extremely
lengthy, and as a result more time will be required to bring these discussions to a
satisfactory conclusion.
1.1.5.  For this reason, the Applicant has decided to consult on a new Proposal which will
support the Airport’s medium-term growth requirements without jeopardising its long-
term future.
1.1.6.  As part of this Proposal, the Applicant is seeking to increase non-weekday (i.e.
weekends and public holidays) aircraft movements at the Airport within its current limit
of 50,000 aircraft movements per annum (pa), amend the maximum take-off weight
(MTOW) categories, and amend the conditions related to airport public safety zones
(PSZs) in line with the latest Government guidance, by varying the conditions
attached to planning permission reference 20/00871/REVPP1 (hereafter referred to as
‘the Proposal’). Amending these conditions would enable the Airport to continue to
meet future market demand for business aviation activity.
1.1.7.  The 'Site' referred to in this Report is the land within the Airport boundary of
ownership as defined in Figure 2.1: Site Location Plan of Appendix A, with the red
line illustrating the extent of the Site which is hereafter referred to as the 'Site
Boundary'.

1.3.  DEFINITION OF AN EIA
1.3.1.  The term EIA describes a procedure that must be followed for certain types of
projects before they can be given consent. The procedure is a means of drawing
together, in a systematic way, an assessment of a project’s potential significant
environmental effects. This helps to ensure that the importance of the predicted
effects and the scope for avoiding, preventing, reducing or, if possible, offsetting them
are properly understood by the public and the authority granting consent (the
'determining authority') before it makes its decision.

considered to have likely significant effects on the environment by virtue of factors
such as its nature, size or location drawing on Schedule 3.

19902 relating to EIA development. Therefore, the Proposal falls under Schedule 2

commercial buildings and a 169-bedroom hotel with leisure and conference facilities.
