THE AIRPORT’S OPERATIONS
2.1.16.  Flying activity at the Airport is restricted by planning conditions which impose
constraints on its operation. Such restrictions include operating hours, the type and
weight of aircraft and some types of activity, such as:
•  Scheduled passenger services;
•  ‘Inclusive tour’ charter services;
•  Bulk freight services;
•  Flight training; and
•  Recreational flying13.

2.1.17.  The Airport flight operations occur between 07:00 and 22:00 Monday to Friday and
08:00 and 20:00 on non-weekdays. The Applicant recorded a total of 29,702 aircraft
movements in 2024, with a total of 8,261  movements for weekends14. Ground based
operations such as aircraft fuelling is permitted to occur between 05:45 and 22:15
from Monday to Friday and between 07:00 and 20:15 on non  -weekdays. The Airport
is closed on the 25 December and 26 December annually, meaning no ground based
or airborne operations occur on these days.
2.1.18.  There is one runway at the Airport with two directions of use. The direction of arrivals
and departures is dictated by the wind direction. Aircraft depart and arrive  at wind as
this is optimal for aerodynamic and safety reasons. Therefore, the Airport operates in
two directions. These are ‘easterly operations’ for when the wind direction is from the
east and ‘westerly operations’ when the wind direction is from the west. The UK’s
prevailing wind is from a south westerly direction, meaning the Airport operates on
westerly operations for most of the time. The split between westerly and easterly
operations varies year to year, however over the last three years (2022 to 2024)
westerly operations have occurred on average approximately 75% of the time
meaning the arrivals and departures to the east have occurred around 25% of the
time.

OVERARCHING AVIATION NOISE POLICY (2023)
3.5.4.  The Overarching Aviation Noise Policy Statement (OANPS)46 was published on 27
March 2023 and details the Government’s revised overarching aviation noise policy
statement. Its revision is linked to the  Flightpath to the Future47, which acknowledged
that the Government would set out next steps on noise policy in 2022 to 2023.
3.5.5.  The publication of the OANPS46 supported the night-time noise abatement objective
consultation whilst providing clarity for both airports and their stakeholders when
preparing or responding to noise action plan consultations.
3.5.6.  The OANPS46 sets out the Government’s revised overarching aviation noise policy
relating to aviation, as follows:
“The Government’s overall policy on aviation noise is to balance the economic and
consumer benefits of aviation against their social and health implications in line with
the International Civil Aviation Organisation’s Balanced Approach to Aircraft Noise
Management. This should take into account the local and national context of both
passenger and freight operations and recognise the additional health impacts of night
flights. The impact of aviation noise must be mitigated as much as is practicable and
realistic to do so, limiting, and where possible reducing, the total adverse impacts on
health and quality of life from aviation noise”.
3.5.7.  The OANPS46 also refers to a previous consultation, as part of  Aviation 205048, on
setting a new objective “to limit, and where possible, reduce total adverse effects on
health and quality of life from aviation noise”48. The OANPS explains:

“We consider that “limit, and where possible reduce” remains appropriate wording. An
overall reduction in total adverse effects is desirable, but in the context of sustainable
growth an increase in total adverse effects may be offset by an increase in econ  omic
and consumer benefits. In circumstances where there is an increase in total adverse
effects, “limit” would mean to mitigate and minimise adverse effects, in line with the
Noise Policy Statement for England”  46.

3.6.3.  Planning permission was originally granted in 200061 to use the prior airfield site for

control tower, hangars and terminal building.
3.6.4.  This permission removed permitted development rights associated with industrial,
warehousing and Airport related development, with the reason being so that the Local
Planning Authority, RBC, could properly consider the effect of any future proposals on
the character and amenity of the Strategic Gap. Strategic Gaps are designated areas
of open land intended to prevent the coalescence of neighbouring settlements, such
as Farnborough and Aldershot, and to preserve their separate identity, character, and
landscape setting.

4.1.  INTRODUCTION
4.1.1.  This Section sets out the approach the EIA will follow to assess any potential
significant effects as a result of the Proposal. The approach to the EIA has been
informed by the ISEP Environmental Impact Assessment Guide to: Delivering Quality
Development77 and the Planning Practice Guidance for EIAs78, and follows the
approach that was taken for the 2023 Planning Application. A detailed overview of the
guidance and methodology adopted for each environmental discipline is provided
within the respective sections of this Report.
4.1.2.  This Scoping Report constitutes a formal Scoping Opinion request from RBC for the
Proposal in accordance with Regulation 15 of the  EIA Regulations3 to identify:

•  The people and environmental resources (collectively known as 'receptors') that
could be significantly affected by the Proposal; and
•  The work required to take forward the assessment of these potential significant
effects.
4.1.3.  Of these effects, those that were identified as being likely to be significant are
proposed to be assessed in the EIA. This reflects the requirement of the  EIA
Regulations3 for the ES to document the likely significant effects of development.

4.1.4.  The ES will contain the information specified in Regulation 18 and Schedule 4 of the
EIA Regulations3.

4.2.  DEFINING THE STUDY AREA AND BASELINE CONDITIONS
4.2.1.  The study area for each environmental discipline will be based on the geographical
scope of the potential for likely significant effects relevant to the discipline or the
information required to assess the potential likely significant effects, as well as
specific guidance and consultation with stakeholders.

4.3.  APPROACH TO ESTABLISHING THE BASELINE FOR THE
ASSESSMENT

CURRENT STATE OF THE ENVIRONMENT
4.3.1.  Baseline environmental conditions need to be established to enable an accurate
assessment of potential changes to such conditions which may occur and to assess
the potential significant environmental effects of the Proposal. Understanding baseline
conditions is also important for the identification of the most appropriate
environmental measures which could be adopted to reduce any potential significant
adverse effects.
4.3.2.  The EIA Regulations3 require an ES to describe the current state of the environment.
This information will be gathered through desk-based research, site surveys and
information available at the time of the assessment, to define and describe the
existing environmental characteristics and receptors for each environmental
discipline.
4.3.3.  Operational data from 2024 will generally be used to describe the current state of the
environment to provide a typical description of the Airport’s operations. There may be
some situations, namely traffic and transport, where the current state of the
environment will be extrapolated using a growth forecast on existing survey data.

APPROACH TO ESTABLISHING FUTURE BASELINE CONDITIONS FOR THE
ASSESSMENT
4.3.4.  It is recognised that the Airport is not operating at the approved 50,000 aircraft
movements pa. Therefore, should the EIA compare the environmental effects of the
proposed 13,500 aircraft movements pa during non-weekdays to the current state of
the environment, it would not be clear which part of the environmental effect resulted
from increasing the non-weekday cap on aircraft movements and which part related to
expanded operations within the existing cap.
4.3.5.  The EIA Regulations3 require an outline of the likely evolution of the baseline
conditions without implementation of the Proposal. Future baseline conditions and
appropriate assumptions will be used to inform the EIA in assessing likely future
conditions should the Proposal not proceed. This is termed as the ‘Without Proposal’
scenario. The future baseline conditions will be described in each technical chapter of
the ES.
4.3.6.  As such, and to provide a transparent assessment, the 'With Proposal’ and ‘Without
Proposal’ scenarios will be identified to underpin the EIA. These scenarios will be
based on the most robust data available and based on the Applicant’s projections for
growth, policy outlined in Section 3.3, market signals and professional judgement
through consultation with recognised industry experts.
4.3.7.  The scenarios will clearly set out how operations at the Airport will likely evolve based
firstly on the 2011 Planning Permission17 (the ‘Without Proposal’ scenario) and
secondly with the Proposal (the  ‘With Proposal’ scenario), see below for further
details. Comparing the With Proposal scenario with the Without Proposal scenario will
allow the effects of the Proposal to be readily identified for each assessment year.
4.3.8.  Data for the Without Proposal scenario will be used as the basis of the assessment
for relevant assessment years. Future baseline conditions will be identified through
modelling/predictions to identify future environmental conditions that can form the
basis to assess the future effects of the Proposal. For example, the noise assessment
will predict noise conditions at and in the vicinity of the Airport for the Without
Proposal scenario. These noise conditions will then be compared with the noise
conditions in the same year for the With Proposal scenario to identify the potential
significant effects of the Proposal for that year.

ASSESSMENT YEARS
4.3.9.  The Proposal does not include any physical works. Therefore, there is no
construction/demolition (or decommissioning) for the EIA to assess. As such, the EIA
will only consider the operational effects of the Proposal.
4.3.10.  It is recognised however that the operational effects of the Proposal may vary over
time due to the differences between the With and Without Proposal scenarios. To
provide a robust assessment of each of the potential significant effects of the
Proposal a range of assessment years will be considered.
4.3.11.  The Principal Assessment Year will be 2045 as this is the year that the approved
aircraft movements cap would be reached without the Proposal (i.e. the Without
Proposal scenario).
4.3.12.  Two interim assessment years will be considered to support a robust assessment for
each environmental discipline, recognising the differing guidance and context for each
assessment:
•  Interim Assessment Year 2033 – The assessments will consider 2033 as the
year likely to have the greatest increase in aircraft movements between the With
and Without Proposal scenarios;
•  Interim Assessment Year 2034 – The assessments will consider 2034 as the
year the approved aircraft movements cap with the Proposal is likely to be
reached; and
•  The climate change assessment will consider assessment years based on the
UK’s carbon budget.

proposed development. The local planning authorities should always have regard to

residual (post-mitigation) environmental effects of the Proposal affecting the same
receptor.

# How life has changed in North Tyneside: Census 2021

  

North Tyneside's population increased by around 8,200 between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021). This semi-automated article highlights some of the most notable changes among the local population.

## The population reached nearly 210,000

Between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021), the population of North Tyneside increased by 4.1%, from just over 200,800 in 2011 to around 209,000 in 2021.

This means North Tyneside's population saw the second-largest percentage increase in the North East, behind [Newcastle upon Tyne](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censusareachanges/E08000021) (where the population increased by 7.1%). The population of the North East increased by 1.9%, while the population of England rose by 6.6%.

In 2021, North Tyneside was home to around 18.1 people per football pitch-sized piece of land, compared with 17.4 in 2011. This area was the third-most densely populated local authority area across the North East (after [Middlesbrough](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censusareachanges/E06000002) and Newcastle upon Tyne).

This article generally uses percentages to enable comparisons over time and between areas. The percentage point change is also used to show the difference between the 2011 and 2021 percentages.

## An older North Tyneside

Between the last two censuses, the average (median) age of North Tyneside increased by two years, from 41 to 43 years of age.

This area had a slightly higher average (median) age than the North East as a whole in 2021 (42 years) and a higher average (median) age than England (40 years).

The median age is the age of the person in the middle of the group, meaning that one half of the group is younger than that person and the other half is older.

The number of people aged 65 to 74 years rose by around 5,900 (an increase of 32.5%), while the number of residents between 35 and 49 years fell by around 2,500 (5.7% decrease).

## Religion in North Tyneside

In 2021, 46.1% of North Tyneside residents reported having "No religion", up from 28.1% in 2011. The rise of 18.0 percentage points was the largest increase of all broad religious groups in North Tyneside. Because the census question about religious affiliation is voluntary and has varying response rates, caution is needed when comparing figures between different areas or between censuses.

Across the North East, the percentage of residents who described themselves as having "No religion" increased from 23.4% to 40.0%, while across England the percentage increased from 24.8% to 36.7%.

In 2021, 46.6% of people in North Tyneside described themselves as Christian (down from 63.8%), while 4.8% did not state their religion (down from 6.4% the decade before).

There are many factors that can cause changes to the religious profile of an area, such as a changing age structure or residents relocating for work or education. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses. Religious affiliation is the religion with which someone connects or identifies, rather than their beliefs or religious practice.

[Read the bulletin Religion, England and Wales: Census 2021.](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/culturalidentity/religion/bulletins/religionenglandandwales/census2021)

## People looking after their family or home in North Tyneside

In 2021, 3.9% of North Tyneside residents (aged 16 years and over) said they were economically inactive because they were looking after their family or home. This figure increased from 3.1% in 2011.

This area had the region’s second lowest percentage of people who were economically inactive because they were looking after their family or home. Across the region, only [Northumberland](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censusareachanges/E06000057), with 3.8%, had a lower percentage.

Census 2021 took place during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, a period of rapid and unparalleled change; the national lockdown, associated guidance and furlough measures will have affected the labour market and our ability to measure it.

## Fewer adults working long hours

North Tyneside saw the North East's joint second-largest percentage-point fall (alongside [South Tyneside](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censusareachanges/E08000023)) in the proportion of people aged 16 years and over and in employment who said they usually worked over 49 hours per week (from 10.3% in 2011 to 8.4% in 2021).

## Ethnic groups in North Tyneside

In 2021, 2.6% of North Tyneside residents identified their ethnic group within the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" category, up from 1.9% in 2011. The 0.7 percentage-point change was the largest increase among high-level ethnic groups in this area.

Across the North East, the percentage of people from the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" ethnic group increased from 2.9% to 3.7%, while across England the percentage increased from 7.8% to 9.6%.

In 2021, 94.9% of people in North Tyneside identified their ethnic group within the "White" category (compared with 96.6% in 2011), while 1.4% identified their ethnic group within the "Mixed or Multiple" category (compared with 0.9% the previous decade).

The percentage of people who identified their ethnic group within the "Other" category ("Arab" or "Any other ethnic group") increased from 0.2% in 2011 to 0.6% in 2021.

There are many factors that may be contributing to the changing ethnic composition of England and Wales, such as differing patterns of ageing, fertility, mortality, and migration. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses.

## About the data

Census data are adjusted to reflect estimated non-response so that the published results relate to the entire usually resident population as it was on Census Day (21 March 2021).

Those respondents who were on furlough because of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic were asked to classify themselves as "temporarily away from work" to ensure they remained in the economically active population.

Students are counted as usually resident at their term-time address even if they were not physically present there on Census Day.

The questions relating to disability differed slightly between 2011 and 2021 to ensure that data were more closely aligned with the definition of disability in the Equality Act (2010). There was also a change to question wording for unpaid care, for more information read the [health, disability and unpaid care quality information](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/healthandwellbeing/methodologies/healthdisabilityandunpaidcarequalityinformationforcensus2021).

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout the health, disability and unpaid care sections. They allow for fairer comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure. The 2013 European Standard Population is used to standardise proportions.

Percentages and percentage point changes have been individually rounded to one decimal place. This means they may not sum exactly.

## About these articles

There is an article like this for every local authority district in England and Wales. The articles have been written and semi-automated by our data journalists and are a new publishing format for the Office for National Statistics.

Topics are chosen and ordered automatically based on how relevant they are for each area, however all data are checked before publishing.

We have not included topics that were new for Census 2021 or where there is no comparability with the 2011 Census. Read about [how we developed and tested the questions for Census 2021](https://www.ons.gov.uk/census/planningforcensus2021/questiondevelopment).

These articles were first published on 8 December 2022 covering topics such as demography, country of birth, ethnic groups, religion, national identity and economic activity status. They were updated on 19 January 2023 following the release of more data from Census 2021 and now include housing tenure, general health, disability and unpaid care.

# How life has changed in North Tyneside: Census 2021

  

North Tyneside's population increased by around 8,200 between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021). This semi-automated article highlights some of the most notable changes among the local population.

  

Choose an area **Select an alternative area**

19 January 2023

  

## The population reached nearly 210,000

Between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021), the population of North Tyneside increased by 4.1%, from just over 200,800 in 2011 to around 209,000 in 2021.

This means North Tyneside's population saw the second-largest percentage increase in the North East, behind [Newcastle upon Tyne](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censusareachanges/E08000021) (where the population increased by 7.1%). The population of the North East increased by 1.9%, while the population of England rose by 6.6%.

In 2021, North Tyneside was home to around 18.1 people per football pitch-sized piece of land, compared with 17.4 in 2011. This area was the third-most densely populated local authority area across the North East (after [Middlesbrough](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censusareachanges/E06000002) and Newcastle upon Tyne).

This article generally uses percentages to enable comparisons over time and between areas. The percentage point change is also used to show the difference between the 2011 and 2021 percentages.

## An older North Tyneside

Between the last two censuses, the average (median) age of North Tyneside increased by two years, from 41 to 43 years of age.

## Religion in North Tyneside

In 2021, 46.1% of North Tyneside residents reported having "No religion", up from 28.1% in 2011. The rise of 18.0 percentage points was the largest increase of all broad religious groups in North Tyneside. Because the census question about religious affiliation is voluntary and has varying response rates, caution is needed when comparing figures between different areas or between censuses.

Across the North East, the percentage of residents who described themselves as having "No religion" increased from 23.4% to 40.0%, while across England the percentage increased from 24.8% to 36.7%.

In 2021, 46.6% of people in North Tyneside described themselves as Christian (down from 63.8%), while 4.8% did not state their religion (down from 6.4% the decade before).

There are many factors that can cause changes to the religious profile of an area, such as a changing age structure or residents relocating for work or education. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses. Religious affiliation is the religion with which someone connects or identifies, rather than their beliefs or religious practice.

[Read the bulletin Religion, England and Wales: Census 2021.](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/culturalidentity/religion/bulletins/religionenglandandwales/census2021)

## Disability in North Tyneside

In 2021, 8.6% of North Tyneside residents were identified as being disabled and limited a lot. This figure decreased from 10.4% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

In 2021, just over one in nine people (11.2%) were identified as being disabled and limited a little, compared with 10.9% in 2011. The proportion of North Tyneside residents who were not disabled increased from 78.7% to 80.3%.

This area had the region’s third lowest proportion of residents who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot. Across the region, only Northumberland (8.3%) and Darlington (8.4%) had a lower proportion of residents who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived their health status and activity limitations, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

## Ethnic groups in North Tyneside

In 2021, 2.6% of North Tyneside residents identified their ethnic group within the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" category, up from 1.9% in 2011. The 0.7 percentage-point change was the largest increase among high-level ethnic groups in this area.

Across the North East, the percentage of people from the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" ethnic group increased from 2.9% to 3.7%, while across England the percentage increased from 7.8% to 9.6%.

In 2021, 94.9% of people in North Tyneside identified their ethnic group within the "White" category (compared with 96.6% in 2011), while 1.4% identified their ethnic group within the "Mixed or Multiple" category (compared with 0.9% the previous decade).

The percentage of people who identified their ethnic group within the "Other" category ("Arab" or "Any other ethnic group") increased from 0.2% in 2011 to 0.6% in 2021.

There are many factors that may be contributing to the changing ethnic composition of England and Wales, such as differing patterns of ageing, fertility, mortality, and migration. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses.

## About the data

Census data are adjusted to reflect estimated non-response so that the published results relate to the entire usually resident population as it was on Census Day (21 March 2021).

Those respondents who were on furlough because of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic were asked to classify themselves as "temporarily away from work" to ensure they remained in the economically active population.

Students are counted as usually resident at their term-time address even if they were not physically present there on Census Day.

The questions relating to disability differed slightly between 2011 and 2021 to ensure that data were more closely aligned with the definition of disability in the Equality Act (2010). There was also a change to question wording for unpaid care, for more information read the [health, disability and unpaid care quality information](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/healthandwellbeing/methodologies/healthdisabilityandunpaidcarequalityinformationforcensus2021).

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout the health, disability and unpaid care sections. They allow for fairer comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure. The 2013 European Standard Population is used to standardise proportions.

Percentages and percentage point changes have been individually rounded to one decimal place. This means they may not sum exactly.

## About these articles

There is an article like this for every local authority district in England and Wales. The articles have been written and semi-automated by our data journalists and are a new publishing format for the Office for National Statistics.

Topics are chosen and ordered automatically based on how relevant they are for each area, however all data are checked before publishing.

We have not included topics that were new for Census 2021 or where there is no comparability with the 2011 Census. Read about [how we developed and tested the questions for Census 2021](https://www.ons.gov.uk/census/planningforcensus2021/questiondevelopment).

These articles were first published on 8 December 2022 covering topics such as demography, country of birth, ethnic groups, religion, national identity and economic activity status. They were updated on 19 January 2023 following the release of more data from Census 2021 and now include housing tenure, general health, disability and unpaid care.

# Population by age (2021 Census)

Census 2021 data showing population by age group in the North East.

 Census 2021

[Download as a PDF](javascript:window.print();)

* * *

Statistics about the age of the population and the geographical distribution of people in different age groups provide valuable insights for a range of data users.

A key role is in planning and funding local government services that focus on children or older workers or the over-80s, for example. The small area data, in particular, shows concentrations of different age groups within parts of North East local authority areas.

**The North East population in 2021**

In March 2021, at the time of the census, the resident population was 1,969,797. The median age was 42 and the five single years of age with the highest populations were those from 55 to 59.

**Comparisons of age structures in different areas**

Among the seven North East local authority areas:

*   About 26.5% of the census resident population was in County Durham
*   Northumberland (16.3%) and Newcastle (15.2%) had the next highest populations
*   County Durham had the highest population in each broad age group
*   Northumberland had the second highest population among the 0 to 15 and 45 and over age groups
*   Newcastle had the second highest population among the 16 to 44 age groups.

Compared to England excluding London, the North East had a higher percentage of its population among broad age groups aged 55 to 84 and among those aged 16 to 24. The latter partly reflecting the presence of students at four universities.

Among the eight core city LEP areas, the North East had:

*   The lowest percentage of its population within each broad age group from 0 to 44 and
*   the highest percentage among each age group from 55 upwards.

Within the North East:

*   North Tyneside had the highest percentages of its population aged 0 to 15 and aged 35 to 54
*   Newcastle had the highest percentages aged 16 to 34 and
*   Northumberland the highest in all age groups aged 55 and over.

**Changes since the 2011 census**

The North East population in 2021 was about 35,700 higher than 10 years earlier. During this period, the population decreased within three broad age groups. These were the 16 to 24, 35 to 44 and 45 to 54 age groups. The population fell in all seven local authority areas for the oldest of these age groups and in all areas except Newcastle for the other two.

The 10-year percentage growth in the North East population (1.8%) was less than a third of that of England excluding London (6.4%). In the age groups with population growth, the North East percentage increase was lower than that of England excluding London in most cases. The exceptions were the 65 to 74 and 85 plus age groups. In age groups with a falling North East population, the percentage decrease was much higher than in England excluding London.

The percentage increase in the North East population was the lowest among the eight core city LEP areas. Within the North East, 10-year percentage increases in total population were highest in Newcastle and North Tyneside. There were percentage decreases in Gateshead, Sunderland and South Tyneside.

* * *

**Implications for annual mid-year population estimates**

The census population statistics are used as a basis for the annual mid-year population estimates over the following decade. They also feed into retrospective revisions to estimates during the previous decade.

The mid-2021 estimates have been released, based on the latest census and they show disparities with the mid-2020 estimates, at a local authority area level in particular. The revised estimates for the years leading up to 2021 are due to be released in the first half of 2023.

There is more information about the latest North East mid-year estimates on the [Evidence Hub population page](https://evidencehub.northeastlep.co.uk/report/population-by-age-group "Mid year population by age group").

# Population by age (2021 Census)

Census 2021 data showing population by age group in the North East.

 Census 2021

[Download as a PDF](javascript:window.print();)

* * *

Statistics about the age of the population and the geographical distribution of people in different age groups provide valuable insights for a range of data users.

A key role is in planning and funding local government services that focus on children or older workers or the over-80s, for example. The small area data, in particular, shows concentrations of different age groups within parts of North East local authority areas.

**The North East population in 2021**

In March 2021, at the time of the census, the resident population was 1,969,797. The median age was 42 and the five single years of age with the highest populations were those from 55 to 59.

* * *

**Comparisons of age structures in different areas**

Among the seven North East local authority areas:

*   About 26.5% of the census resident population was in County Durham
*   Northumberland (16.3%) and Newcastle (15.2%) had the next highest populations
*   County Durham had the highest population in each broad age group
*   Northumberland had the second highest population among the 0 to 15 and 45 and over age groups
*   Newcastle had the second highest population among the 16 to 44 age groups.

Compared to England excluding London, the North East had a higher percentage of its population among broad age groups aged 55 to 84 and among those aged 16 to 24. The latter partly reflecting the presence of students at four universities.

Among the eight core city LEP areas, the North East had:

*   The lowest percentage of its population within each broad age group from 0 to 44 and
*   the highest percentage among each age group from 55 upwards.

Within the North East:

*   North Tyneside had the highest percentages of its population aged 0 to 15 and aged 35 to 54
*   Newcastle had the highest percentages aged 16 to 34 and
*   Northumberland the highest in all age groups aged 55 and over.

* * *

**Changes since the 2011 census**

The North East population in 2021 was about 35,700 higher than 10 years earlier. During this period, the population decreased within three broad age groups. These were the 16 to 24, 35 to 44 and 45 to 54 age groups. The population fell in all seven local authority areas for the oldest of these age groups and in all areas except Newcastle for the other two.

The 10-year percentage growth in the North East population (1.8%) was less than a third of that of England excluding London (6.4%). In the age groups with population growth, the North East percentage increase was lower than that of England excluding London in most cases. The exceptions were the 65 to 74 and 85 plus age groups. In age groups with a falling North East population, the percentage decrease was much higher than in England excluding London.

The percentage increase in the North East population was the lowest among the eight core city LEP areas. Within the North East, 10-year percentage increases in total population were highest in Newcastle and North Tyneside. There were percentage decreases in Gateshead, Sunderland and South Tyneside.

* * *

**Implications for annual mid-year population estimates**

The census population statistics are used as a basis for the annual mid-year population estimates over the following decade. They also feed into retrospective revisions to estimates during the previous decade.

The mid-2021 estimates have been released, based on the latest census and they show disparities with the mid-2020 estimates, at a local authority area level in particular. The revised estimates for the years leading up to 2021 are due to be released in the first half of 2023.

There is more information about the latest North East mid-year estimates on the [Evidence Hub population page](https://evidencehub.northeastlep.co.uk/report/population-by-age-group "Mid year population by age group").

* * *

**Mapping population by age in small areas**

The ONS interactive census map shown below is embedded in this and other Evidence Hub pages. It allows users to view geographical patterns in census datasets interactively.

We have set up the map to show the percentage of each local authority area's population that was aged 55 to 64 in 2021, the adult age group with the highest North East population. However, the age group can be changed using the controls to the left of the map. In addition, the zoom function can be used to view patterns for small areas for each age group.

For more information about this mapping tool, visit the [ONS website](https://www.ons.gov.uk/census/maps "ONS census maps").

# How the population changed in North Tyneside: Census 2021

28 June 2022

  
  

The population of England and Wales has increased by more than 3.5 million in the 10 years leading up to Census 2021. Using the first results from this census, we look at which places have seen the biggest increases and decreases, which areas had the largest growth in different age groups, and how local authority areas like North Tyneside compare with others.

## The population of England and Wales is the largest ever recorded

  
There were 59,597,300 people living in England and Wales on 21 March 2021, the day of the latest census. This is over 3.5 million more (6.3%) than in 2011 and is the largest census population ever recorded.

* * *

### Population change (%) in **English regions** and **Wales** between 2011 and 2021

Percentage growth

The English region with the largest population increase was the East of England, which grew by around 8.3% or 488,000 more residents. The English region with the smallest increase was the North East, growing by 1.9% or around 50,000 people. In Wales, the population grew by 1.4% or 44,000 people.

A map shows the English regions and Wales.

In North Tyneside, the population size has increased by 4.1%, from around 200,800 in 2011 to 209,000 in 2021. This is lower than the overall increase for England (6.6%), where the population grew by nearly 3.5 million to 56,489,800.

A map of local authority areas in England is coloured to indicate the percentage change in population of each area. The data used in this article are available to download at the end.

Nearby areas like [Newcastle upon Tyne](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E08000021) and [Northumberland](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E06000057) have seen their populations increase by around 7.1% and 1.4%, respectively, while others such as [Gateshead](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E08000037) and [South Tyneside](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E08000023) have seen decreases of 2.1% and 0.2%, respectively.

The map then zooms to centre on North Tyneside and show neighbouring areas.

The largest population increases in the North East have been seen in [Newcastle upon Tyne](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E08000021) and North Tyneside, where the populations have grown by 7.1% and 4.1%, respectively.

The map zooms out to show the percentage change in population size in all local authority areas in the North East

At the other end of the scale, [Gateshead](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E08000037) has seen a fall of 2.1%.

The local authority areas displayed on the map change form and position to create a bar chart that orders selected areas of the North East by percentage change in total population.

At 4.1%, North Tyneside's population increase is higher than the increase for the North East (1.9%).

North Tyneside is highlighted on the bar chart along with other local authority areas in the North East.

[Tower Hamlets](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E09000030) saw the largest percentage growth in population in England, increasing 22.1% between 2011 and 2021. [Dartford](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E07000107) was second, increasing 20.0%.

Every local authority area of England is shown as a dot on a chart, with the legend running from the largest percentage decrease to the highest percentage increase in population. North Tyneside is highlighted.

Some local authority areas have seen their populations decline. [Kensington and Chelsea](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E09000020) had an estimated population of 143,400 in 2021, which was around 15,200 fewer than in 2011 and a decrease of 9.6%.

The chart continues to show all areas of England as dots, ordered by the percentage change in total population, with the largest decreases towards the left and the largest increases towards the right.

The total population of local authority areas varies a lot, from [Birmingham](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E08000025) with around 1,144,900 people to [the Isles of Scilly](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E06000053) with around 2,100 people. The sizes of these circles are proportionate to the size of the population in each local authority area.

The chart changes into circles located at the centre of each local authority area on a map. The area of each circle indicates the total population.

## How different local authority areas rank for population size

  
  
In 2021, North Tyneside ranked 89th for total population out of 309 local authority areas in England, which is a fall of one place in a decade.

## There are three people for every football pitch-sized piece of land in England

  
  
There were 434 residents per square kilometre in England in 2021, up from 407 per square kilometre in 2011. Population density varies from area to area. We can see the difference between local authority areas if we measure the land in football pitches and work out how many people there would be on each one. 

As of 2021, North Tyneside is the third most densely populated of the North East's 12 local authority areas, with around 18 people living on each football pitch-sized area of land.

A drawing of a football pitch is displayed. The number of people on the pitch, or the number of pitches for one person, changes as described in the text content.

[Tower Hamlets](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E09000030) in London has become the most densely populated local authority area in England (overtaking [Islington](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E09000019)) with the equivalent of around 112 people per pitch.

At the other end of the population density scale for England, the amount of land in [Eden](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E07000030) in Cumbria works out at around five pitches per resident.

## There were more people than ever aged 65 years and over in England

  
  
The population has continued to age. Across England, more than one in six people (18.4%) were aged 65 years and over on Census Day in 2021. This is a higher percentage than ever before.

### The age and sex distribution of the population of **the North East in 2011**

This population pyramid shows the population of males and females in each five-year age group at the time of the 2011 Census.  
The largest age group in the North East back then was those aged 45 to 49 years.

A population pyramid is displayed. It shows males and females in each age group as a percentage of the total population for North Tyneside in 2011. The age group with the largest number of people is highlighted.

More recently, in 2021, the largest age group in the North East was those aged 55 to 59 years.

A population pyramid is displayed. It shows the number males and females in each age group as a percentage of the total population for the North East in 2021. The age group with the largest number of people is highlighted.

In England, the largest age group in 2021 was people aged 30 to 34 years.

The population pyramid changes to show the number of males and females in each age group as a percentage of the total population in England. The age group with the largest number of people is highlighted.

Overall, in England, there has been an increase of 20.1% in people aged 65 years and over, an increase of 3.6% in people aged 15 to 64 years, and an increase of 5.0% in children aged under 15 years.

The population pyramid turns into a horizontal bar chart, with bars representing the percentage change in the number of people of any sex in each five-year age group in England.

This is how North Tyneside compares. There has been an increase of 21.3% in people aged 65 years and over, a decrease of 0.9% in people aged 15 to 64 years, and an increase of 5.1% in children aged under 15 years.

The horizontal bar chart now shows the percentage change in the number of people of any sex in each five-year age group in North Tyneside.

## The population change in different age groups varies across England

  
  
In 32 of the 309 local authority areas of England, the total number of people aged 65 years and over increased by 30.0% or more between 2011 and 2021. This compares with a 20.1% rise across England.

* * *

### Local authority areas in **England** that have seen an increase of 30% or more in those aged 65 years and over, 2011 to 2021

The places that have seen the largest increases in the population aged 65 years and over are [Milton Keynes](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E06000042/) in the South East, which has seen 43.6% growth, and [Harborough](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E07000131/) in the East Midlands (38.5%).

A map of England appears, highlighting the areas with the largest increases in people aged 65 years and over.

The places that have seen the largest increases in the population aged under 15 years are [Dartford](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E07000107) in Kent, where the size of this age group increased by 31.8% between 2011 and 2021, and [Peterborough](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E06000031) in the East of England (23.8%).

The map now highlights the areas with the largest increases in children aged under 15 years.

The places that have seen the largest percentage decrease in the number of children aged under 15 years are [Westminster](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E09000033/) (19.4%) and [Kensington and Chelsea](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E09000020/) (17.8%) in London and [Richmondshire](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E07000166/) in Yorkshire (12.3%).

The map now highlights the areas with the largest decreases in children aged under 15 years.

# How the population changed in North Tyneside: Census 2021

28 June 2022

  
  

The population of England and Wales has increased by more than 3.5 million in the 10 years leading up to Census 2021. Using the first results from this census, we look at which places have seen the biggest increases and decreases, which areas had the largest growth in different age groups, and how local authority areas like North Tyneside compare with others.

## The population of England and Wales is the largest ever recorded

  
There were 59,597,300 people living in England and Wales on 21 March 2021, the day of the latest census. This is over 3.5 million more (6.3%) than in 2011 and is the largest census population ever recorded.

* * *

### Population change (%) in **English regions** and **Wales** between 2011 and 2021

The English region with the largest population increase was the East of England, which grew by around 8.3% or 488,000 more residents. The English region with the smallest increase was the North East, growing by 1.9% or around 50,000 people. In Wales, the population grew by 1.4% or 44,000 people.

A map shows the English regions and Wales.

In North Tyneside, the population size has increased by 4.1%, from around 200,800 in 2011 to 209,000 in 2021. This is lower than the overall increase for England (6.6%), where the population grew by nearly 3.5 million to 56,489,800.

A map of local authority areas in England is coloured to indicate the percentage change in population of each area. The data used in this article are available to download at the end.

Nearby areas like [Newcastle upon Tyne](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E08000021) and [Northumberland](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E06000057) have seen their populations increase by around 7.1% and 1.4%, respectively, while others such as [Gateshead](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E08000037) and [South Tyneside](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E08000023) have seen decreases of 2.1% and 0.2%, respectively.

The map then zooms to centre on North Tyneside and show neighbouring areas.

The largest population increases in the North East have been seen in [Newcastle upon Tyne](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E08000021) and North Tyneside, where the populations have grown by 7.1% and 4.1%, respectively.

The map zooms out to show the percentage change in population size in all local authority areas in the North East

At the other end of the scale, [Gateshead](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E08000037) has seen a fall of 2.1%.

The local authority areas displayed on the map change form and position to create a bar chart that orders selected areas of the North East by percentage change in total population.

At 4.1%, North Tyneside's population increase is higher than the increase for the North East (1.9%).

North Tyneside is highlighted on the bar chart along with other local authority areas in the North East.

[Tower Hamlets](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E09000030) saw the largest percentage growth in population in England, increasing 22.1% between 2011 and 2021. [Dartford](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E07000107) was second, increasing 20.0%.

Every local authority area of England is shown as a dot on a chart, with the legend running from the largest percentage decrease to the highest percentage increase in population. North Tyneside is highlighted.

Some local authority areas have seen their populations decline. [Kensington and Chelsea](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E09000020) had an estimated population of 143,400 in 2021, which was around 15,200 fewer than in 2011 and a decrease of 9.6%.

The chart continues to show all areas of England as dots, ordered by the percentage change in total population, with the largest decreases towards the left and the largest increases towards the right.

The total population of local authority areas varies a lot, from [Birmingham](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E08000025) with around 1,144,900 people to [the Isles of Scilly](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E06000053) with around 2,100 people. The sizes of these circles are proportionate to the size of the population in each local authority area.

The chart changes into circles located at the centre of each local authority area on a map. The area of each circle indicates the total population.

## How different local authority areas rank for population size

  
  
In 2021, North Tyneside ranked 89th for total population out of 309 local authority areas in England, which is a fall of one place in a decade.

## There are three people for every football pitch-sized piece of land in England

  
  
There were 434 residents per square kilometre in England in 2021, up from 407 per square kilometre in 2011. Population density varies from area to area. We can see the difference between local authority areas if we measure the land in football pitches and work out how many people there would be on each one. 

As of 2021, North Tyneside is the third most densely populated of the North East's 12 local authority areas, with around 18 people living on each football pitch-sized area of land.

A drawing of a football pitch is displayed. The number of people on the pitch, or the number of pitches for one person, changes as described in the text content.

[Tower Hamlets](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E09000030) in London has become the most densely populated local authority area in England (overtaking [Islington](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E09000019)) with the equivalent of around 112 people per pitch.

At the other end of the population density scale for England, the amount of land in [Eden](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E07000030) in Cumbria works out at around five pitches per resident.

## There were more people than ever aged 65 years and over in England

  
  
The population has continued to age. Across England, more than one in six people (18.4%) were aged 65 years and over on Census Day in 2021. This is a higher percentage than ever before.

* * *

### The age and sex distribution of the population of **the North East in 2011**

This population pyramid shows the population of males and females in each five-year age group at the time of the 2011 Census.  
The largest age group in the North East back then was those aged 45 to 49 years.

A population pyramid is displayed. It shows males and females in each age group as a percentage of the total population for North Tyneside in 2011. The age group with the largest number of people is highlighted.

More recently, in 2021, the largest age group in the North East was those aged 55 to 59 years.

A population pyramid is displayed. It shows the number males and females in each age group as a percentage of the total population for the North East in 2021. The age group with the largest number of people is highlighted.

In England, the largest age group in 2021 was people aged 30 to 34 years.

The population pyramid changes to show the number of males and females in each age group as a percentage of the total population in England. The age group with the largest number of people is highlighted.

Overall, in England, there has been an increase of 20.1% in people aged 65 years and over, an increase of 3.6% in people aged 15 to 64 years, and an increase of 5.0% in children aged under 15 years.

The population pyramid turns into a horizontal bar chart, with bars representing the percentage change in the number of people of any sex in each five-year age group in England.

This is how North Tyneside compares. There has been an increase of 21.3% in people aged 65 years and over, a decrease of 0.9% in people aged 15 to 64 years, and an increase of 5.1% in children aged under 15 years.

The horizontal bar chart now shows the percentage change in the number of people of any sex in each five-year age group in North Tyneside.

## The population change in different age groups varies across England

  
  
In 32 of the 309 local authority areas of England, the total number of people aged 65 years and over increased by 30.0% or more between 2011 and 2021. This compares with a 20.1% rise across England.

* * *

### Local authority areas in **England** that have seen an increase of 30% or more in those aged 65 years and over, 2011 to 2021

The places that have seen the largest increases in the population aged 65 years and over are [Milton Keynes](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E06000042/) in the South East, which has seen 43.6% growth, and [Harborough](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E07000131/) in the East Midlands (38.5%).

A map of England appears, highlighting the areas with the largest increases in people aged 65 years and over.

The places that have seen the largest increases in the population aged under 15 years are [Dartford](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E07000107) in Kent, where the size of this age group increased by 31.8% between 2011 and 2021, and [Peterborough](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E06000031) in the East of England (23.8%).

The map now highlights the areas with the largest increases in children aged under 15 years.

The places that have seen the largest percentage decrease in the number of children aged under 15 years are [Westminster](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E09000033/) (19.4%) and [Kensington and Chelsea](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E09000020/) (17.8%) in London and [Richmondshire](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/censuspopulationchange/E07000166/) in Yorkshire (12.3%).

The map now highlights the areas with the largest decreases in children aged under 15 years.

Population change in certain areas may reflect how the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic affected people's choice of usual residence on Census Day, for example, students and in some urban areas.

### Two-model comparison: White British, 2051

±2.1pp spread

Hamilton-Perry (HP) central 82.1%Cohort change ratios from Census 2011 to 2021. Demographic momentum only, no fertility convergence.

Cohort-component 84.2%Births by ethnicity-specific total fertility rate (TFR) with half-convergence to the national mean by 2061. Slower change.

Two independent models trained on the same Census base disagree by 2.1pp on White British share in North Tyneside by 2051. HP captures observed 2011 to 2021 cohort dynamics. The cohort-component model adds explicit fertility assumptions that pull projections toward the national mean. The chart above shows HP. ## How NHS care for overseas residents is funded (national context)

Most non-UK residents in North Tyneside pay for NHS care up-front through the Immigration Health Surcharge (IHS), which is added to most visa applications. **North Tyneside** is a [metropolitan borough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_borough "Metropolitan borough") in the [metropolitan county](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_county "Metropolitan county") of [Tyne and Wear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyne_and_Wear "Tyne and Wear"), [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England"). It forms part of the greater [Tyneside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyneside "Tyneside")[conurbation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conurbation "Conurbation"). [North Tyneside Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside_Council "North Tyneside Council") is headquartered at [Cobalt Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobalt_Park "Cobalt Park"), [Wallsend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallsend "Wallsend").

North Tyneside is bordered by [Newcastle upon Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Newcastle upon Tyne") to the west, the [North Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Sea "North Sea") to the east, the [River Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Tyne "River Tyne") to the south and [Northumberland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumberland "Northumberland") to the north. Within its bounds are the towns of Wallsend, [North Shields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Shields "North Shields"), [Killingworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killingworth "Killingworth"), [Tynemouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tynemouth "Tynemouth") and [Whitley Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitley_Bay "Whitley Bay"), which form a continuously built-up area contiguous with [Newcastle upon Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Newcastle upon Tyne").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_Tyneside&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The borough was formed on 1 April 1974 by the merger of the [county borough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_borough "County borough") of [Tynemouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tynemouth "Tynemouth"), with the borough of [Wallsend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallsend "Wallsend"), part of the borough of [Whitley Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitley_Bay "Whitley Bay"), the [urban district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_district_(Great_Britain_and_Ireland) "Urban district (Great Britain and Ireland)") of [Longbenton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longbenton "Longbenton") and part of the urban district of [Seaton Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seaton_Valley_Urban_District "Seaton Valley Urban District"), all of which were in [Northumberland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumberland "Northumberland"). Killingworth was built as a [new town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_town "New town") in the 1960s and became part of North Tyneside.

## Governance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_Tyneside&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Governance")]

Main article: [North Tyneside Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside_Council "North Tyneside Council")

Unlike most English districts, [North Tyneside Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside_Council "North Tyneside Council") is led by a [directly elected mayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directly_elected_mayors_in_England "Directly elected mayors in England"); since May 2013, this post has been held by [Norma Redfearn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norma_Redfearn "Norma Redfearn") of the [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)"). She was most recently elected on 6 May 2021.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside#cite_note-5)

The council has sixty elected members, three from each of the twenty wards in the borough. [Elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside_Metropolitan_Borough_Council_elections "North Tyneside Metropolitan Borough Council elections") are staggered into thirds, with one councillor from each ward elected each year for three consecutive years, and the mayoral election held on the fourth year.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside#cite_note-6)

North Tyneside is part of the [North East Mayoral Combined Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_Mayoral_Combined_Authority "North East Mayoral Combined Authority"), which is chaired by the directly elected [Mayor of the North East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_the_North_East "Mayor of the North East"); there are therefore two directly elected mayors covering North Tyneside. The combined authority was established in 2024 covering North Tyneside, [County Durham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Durham_(district) "County Durham (district)"), [Gateshead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Borough_of_Gateshead "Metropolitan Borough of Gateshead"), [Newcastle upon Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Newcastle upon Tyne"), [Northumberland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumberland "Northumberland"), [South Tyneside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Tyneside "South Tyneside") and [Sunderland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_Sunderland "City of Sunderland").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside#cite_note-7)

## Economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_Tyneside&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Economy")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Tynemouth%2C_6_January_2012_%285%29.jpg/250px-Tynemouth%2C_6_January_2012_%285%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tynemouth,_6_January_2012_(5).jpg)

[Tynemouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tynemouth "Tynemouth"), one of the towns of the borough

North Tyneside lies in the coalfield that covers the South-East of the historic county of Northumberland. It has traditionally been a centre of [heavy industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_industry "Heavy industry") along with the rest of Tyneside, with for example the [Swan Hunter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swan_Hunter "Swan Hunter") shipyard in Wallsend, and export of coal. Today most of the heavy industry has gone, leaving high unemployment in some areas (over the borough, 5.1% compared to 3.7% for the UK in 2022).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside#cite_note-8)

## Transport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_Tyneside&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Transport")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Tyne_Tunnel_North_Entrance_-_geograph.org.uk_-_149562.jpg/250px-Tyne_Tunnel_North_Entrance_-_geograph.org.uk_-_149562.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tyne_Tunnel_North_Entrance_-_geograph.org.uk_-_149562.jpg)

Tyne Tunnel Southern Entrance

Two key roads serve North Tyneside:

*   The [A19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A19_road "A19 road") which leaves the [A1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A1_road_(Great_Britain) "A1 road (Great Britain)") north of Newcastle and runs through the borough and then through the [Tyne Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyne_Tunnel "Tyne Tunnel") to [South Tyneside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Tyneside "South Tyneside"), [Teesside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teesside "Teesside") and towards the South.
*   The [Coast Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coast_Road "Coast Road") (A1058) runs from Newcastle to the coast. For most of its length it is grade-separated.

North Tyneside is served by 17 stations on the [Tyne and Wear Metro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyne_and_Wear_Metro "Tyne and Wear Metro") on a loop from Newcastle through Wallsend, North Shields, Whitley Bay, Benton and back to Newcastle. Trains operate at least every 15 minutes, with extra services in the peak hours. Most of the stations serving North Tyneside fall into fare zones B and C.

There are no [National Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rail "National Rail") stations in the borough, despite the [East Coast Main Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Coast_Main_Line "East Coast Main Line") and Blyth and Tyne routes passing through. The nearest National Rail stations are Cramlington, Manors and [Newcastle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_railway_station "Newcastle railway station"), which is also served by the Tyne & Wear Metro. [Northumberland Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumberland_Park_Metro_station "Northumberland Park Metro station") will open in 2026 to provide the borough's first heavy rail link since the 1970s.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside#cite_note-9)

North Tyneside has an extensive bus network, with most areas benefiting from direct services to Newcastle. Many areas have direct bus services to Cramlington, Blyth or Morpeth. The principle bus operators in the area are [Arriva North East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arriva_North_East "Arriva North East") (all areas), [Go North East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Go_North_East "Go North East") (most areas) and [Stagecoach in Newcastle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stagecoach_in_Newcastle "Stagecoach in Newcastle") (Benton, Forest Hall, Killingworth and Wallsend).

The [Shields Ferry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shields_Ferry "Shields Ferry") links North Shields to South Shields, in South Tyneside.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside#cite_note-10)

There is an international ferry terminal at [Royal Quays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Quays "Royal Quays") in North Shields, with a service to [Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam "Amsterdam") ([IJmuiden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IJmuiden "IJmuiden")).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside#cite_note-11)

**North Tyneside** is a [metropolitan borough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_borough "Metropolitan borough") in the [metropolitan county](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_county "Metropolitan county") of [Tyne and Wear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyne_and_Wear "Tyne and Wear"), [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England"). It forms part of the greater [Tyneside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyneside "Tyneside")[conurbation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conurbation "Conurbation"). [North Tyneside Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside_Council "North Tyneside Council") is headquartered at [Cobalt Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobalt_Park "Cobalt Park"), [Wallsend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallsend "Wallsend").

North Tyneside is bordered by [Newcastle upon Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Newcastle upon Tyne") to the west, the [North Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Sea "North Sea") to the east, the [River Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Tyne "River Tyne") to the south and [Northumberland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumberland "Northumberland") to the north. Within its bounds are the towns of Wallsend, [North Shields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Shields "North Shields"), [Killingworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killingworth "Killingworth"), [Tynemouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tynemouth "Tynemouth") and [Whitley Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitley_Bay "Whitley Bay"), which form a continuously built-up area contiguous with [Newcastle upon Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Newcastle upon Tyne").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_Tyneside&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The borough was formed on 1 April 1974 by the merger of the [county borough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_borough "County borough") of [Tynemouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tynemouth "Tynemouth"), with the borough of [Wallsend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallsend "Wallsend"), part of the borough of [Whitley Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitley_Bay "Whitley Bay"), the [urban district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_district_(Great_Britain_and_Ireland) "Urban district (Great Britain and Ireland)") of [Longbenton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longbenton "Longbenton") and part of the urban district of [Seaton Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seaton_Valley_Urban_District "Seaton Valley Urban District"), all of which were in [Northumberland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumberland "Northumberland"). Killingworth was built as a [new town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_town "New town") in the 1960s and became part of North Tyneside.

## Governance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_Tyneside&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Governance")]

Main article: [North Tyneside Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside_Council "North Tyneside Council")

Unlike most English districts, [North Tyneside Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside_Council "North Tyneside Council") is led by a [directly elected mayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directly_elected_mayors_in_England "Directly elected mayors in England"); since May 2013, this post has been held by [Norma Redfearn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norma_Redfearn "Norma Redfearn") of the [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)"). She was most recently elected on 6 May 2021.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside#cite_note-5)

The council has sixty elected members, three from each of the twenty wards in the borough. [Elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside_Metropolitan_Borough_Council_elections "North Tyneside Metropolitan Borough Council elections") are staggered into thirds, with one councillor from each ward elected each year for three consecutive years, and the mayoral election held on the fourth year.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside#cite_note-6)

North Tyneside is part of the [North East Mayoral Combined Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_Mayoral_Combined_Authority "North East Mayoral Combined Authority"), which is chaired by the directly elected [Mayor of the North East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_the_North_East "Mayor of the North East"); there are therefore two directly elected mayors covering North Tyneside. The combined authority was established in 2024 covering North Tyneside, [County Durham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Durham_(district) "County Durham (district)"), [Gateshead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Borough_of_Gateshead "Metropolitan Borough of Gateshead"), [Newcastle upon Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Newcastle upon Tyne"), [Northumberland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumberland "Northumberland"), [South Tyneside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Tyneside "South Tyneside") and [Sunderland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_Sunderland "City of Sunderland").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside#cite_note-7)

## Economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_Tyneside&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Economy")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Tynemouth%2C_6_January_2012_%285%29.jpg/250px-Tynemouth%2C_6_January_2012_%285%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tynemouth,_6_January_2012_(5).jpg)

[Tynemouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tynemouth "Tynemouth"), one of the towns of the borough

North Tyneside lies in the coalfield that covers the South-East of the historic county of Northumberland. It has traditionally been a centre of [heavy industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_industry "Heavy industry") along with the rest of Tyneside, with for example the [Swan Hunter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swan_Hunter "Swan Hunter") shipyard in Wallsend, and export of coal. Today most of the heavy industry has gone, leaving high unemployment in some areas (over the borough, 5.1% compared to 3.7% for the UK in 2022).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside#cite_note-8)

## Transport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_Tyneside&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Transport")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Tyne_Tunnel_North_Entrance_-_geograph.org.uk_-_149562.jpg/250px-Tyne_Tunnel_North_Entrance_-_geograph.org.uk_-_149562.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tyne_Tunnel_North_Entrance_-_geograph.org.uk_-_149562.jpg)

Tyne Tunnel Southern Entrance

Two key roads serve North Tyneside:

*   The [A19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A19_road "A19 road") which leaves the [A1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A1_road_(Great_Britain) "A1 road (Great Britain)") north of Newcastle and runs through the borough and then through the [Tyne Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyne_Tunnel "Tyne Tunnel") to [South Tyneside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Tyneside "South Tyneside"), [Teesside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teesside "Teesside") and towards the South.
*   The [Coast Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coast_Road "Coast Road") (A1058) runs from Newcastle to the coast. For most of its length it is grade-separated.

North Tyneside is served by 17 stations on the [Tyne and Wear Metro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyne_and_Wear_Metro "Tyne and Wear Metro") on a loop from Newcastle through Wallsend, North Shields, Whitley Bay, Benton and back to Newcastle. Trains operate at least every 15 minutes, with extra services in the peak hours. Most of the stations serving North Tyneside fall into fare zones B and C.

There are no [National Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rail "National Rail") stations in the borough, despite the [East Coast Main Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Coast_Main_Line "East Coast Main Line") and Blyth and Tyne routes passing through. The nearest National Rail stations are Cramlington, Manors and [Newcastle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_railway_station "Newcastle railway station"), which is also served by the Tyne & Wear Metro. [Northumberland Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumberland_Park_Metro_station "Northumberland Park Metro station") will open in 2026 to provide the borough's first heavy rail link since the 1970s.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside#cite_note-9)

North Tyneside has an extensive bus network, with most areas benefiting from direct services to Newcastle. Many areas have direct bus services to Cramlington, Blyth or Morpeth. The principle bus operators in the area are [Arriva North East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arriva_North_East "Arriva North East") (all areas), [Go North East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Go_North_East "Go North East") (most areas) and [Stagecoach in Newcastle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stagecoach_in_Newcastle "Stagecoach in Newcastle") (Benton, Forest Hall, Killingworth and Wallsend).

The [Shields Ferry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shields_Ferry "Shields Ferry") links North Shields to South Shields, in South Tyneside.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside#cite_note-10)

There is an international ferry terminal at [Royal Quays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Quays "Royal Quays") in North Shields, with a service to [Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam "Amsterdam") ([IJmuiden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IJmuiden "IJmuiden")).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside#cite_note-11)

## Media

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_Tyneside&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Media")]

Local news and television programmes are provided by [BBC North East and Cumbria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_North_East_and_Cumbria "BBC North East and Cumbria") and [ITV Tyne Tees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITV_Tyne_Tees "ITV Tyne Tees"). Television signals are received from the [Pontop Pike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontop_Pike_transmitting_station "Pontop Pike transmitting station") TV transmitter [[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside#cite_note-12)

Radio stations that broadcast to the area are [BBC Radio Newcastle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio_Newcastle "BBC Radio Newcastle"), [Heart North East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_North_East "Heart North East"), [Capital North East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_North_East "Capital North East"), [Smooth Radio North East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_Radio_North_East "Smooth Radio North East"), [Greatest Hits Radio North East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greatest_Hits_Radio_North_East "Greatest Hits Radio North East"), and [Hits Radio North East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hits_Radio_North_East "Hits Radio North East").

The local newspaper is the _[Evening Chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evening\_Chronicle "Evening Chronicle")_.

## Twinned towns

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_Tyneside&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Twinned towns")]

North Tyneside is [twinned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sister_city "Sister city") with:

*   [Oer-Erkenschwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oer-Erkenschwick "Oer-Erkenschwick") in Germany[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside#cite_note-13)
*   [Halluin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halluin "Halluin") in France[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside#cite_note-14)
